div.head: IOACHIMO BELAIO ANTONIVS POSSEVINVS MANTVANVS S. P. D.
div.p: Omnium omnino qui aliquid in lucem redeunt duo genera sunt, alterum eorum à quibus res ipsæ inueniuntur, alterum illorum, qui quod dicturi sunt aliunde assumunt: atque hoc genus in duas parteis rursus distributum est, nam aut qui ab alijs res accipiunt, eas suis uerbis exponunt, aut ad sententias suas aliorum uerba transferunt, atque traducunt, quod quidem pertinet ad eos, qui Centones conscribunt, quo in genere ita mirabilis fuit Lælius Capilupus, ut facilè omnium expectationem uicerit, ac superarit. Nam cum plerumque de rebus ab antiquorum ætate remotissimis agat, eas tamen ita Virgily carminibus tractat, atque complectitur, ut ne ipsum quidem Poëtam supra potuisse existimem. Nam & in dispositione sententiarum, & ordine, & in coniungendis, ac quasi conglutinandis uersibus, qui in Virgilij libris maximo interuallo inter se disiuncti sunt, illud est omnium iudicio consecutus, ut perpetuum potius, et continens scriptum, quàm undique collectum, & comportatum uideatur: in quo uiri illius memoriam, & acre iudicium soleo sæpe admirari, qui res tam dispersas in unum locum cogat, easq; ita collocet, ut media primis, extremis prima respondeant. ac ut perfectus fictor, qui ex diuersissimis lapidibus opus egregium fingit, emblemateq; componit, sic ille ex omnibus Virgilij locis, quæ ad suam sententiam in primis facerent optima quæq; excerpsit, atque libauit, unumq; hoc corpus confecit. Scio autem nonnullos ad hoc scribendi genus se contulisse, in quorum numero apud Græcos fuit

Eudocia ,apud Latinos Proba Falconia, & Ausonius, sed quantum in eo profecerint, aliorum sit iudicium. Illud quidem nec dubitans affirmauerim Lælio non modo in hac re non præstantiores fuisse, sed uix fortasse pares. Nam ut de Ausonio loquar, cum hic de rebus ipsis ageret, facilè illi fuit ad id quod sentiret Poetæ carmina accommodare, longè enim alia notio subijcitur his scriptis, atque illa, quæ Virgilianis subiecta est.

Cum igitur hos Centones sæpissimè legissem, prospiceremq; hunc librum si ederetur iucundissimum omnibus, & utilissimum fore, Lælium rogaui qui mihi potestatem daret ut eum emitterem, quod cum ille ut solet, humanissimè mihi permisisset, nihil mihi antiquius, aut longius fuit, quam ut in manus hominum exiret, etenim præter maximum & uberrimum fructum, quem ex eo quiuis percepturus fuisset, non mediocre commodum me adepturum sciebam, neque.n.dulcius quidquam aut iucundius mihi accidere poterat, quam ut illius scripta proferrentur, quem præterquam quod cum eo summis beneuolentiæ & amicitiæ uinculis sum coniunctus, [printed word struck through in ink, illegible] non modo ob charitatem patriæ quæ illi cum multis est cõmunis , uerùm etiam ob singulares eius uirtutes summo semper amore sum prosecutus. Præterea illud mihi maximo usui futurum uidebam, cum ob hanc causam aditum mihi ad te patefacerem, gratiamq; tuam quodammodo aucuparer. Tu enim is es, qui & summa uirtute præditus, & omnibus literarum studijs ornatissimus Læly Capilupi scripta es adeo admiratus, ut cum ne illum quidem uirum de facie cognosceres, mirificè tamen amares & coleres, quod cum illius ingenio, tum tuæ humanitati & animo ad studia propenso tribuitur. Adeo in humanis animis studia paria possunt, quæ quo sunt liberaliora, eò magis homines inter se quibusdam uinculis deuinciunt, & obstringunt. Quibus rationibus adductus statui hunc librum ad te mittere, quod scirem apud neminem in loco meliore aut honestiore esse posse. Cum enim semper otium, & tempus in discendo contriueris, tum summo illi Cardinali

div.p: es sanguine coniunctus , in quo non facilè iudices utrum mores à disciplinis , an à moribus disciplinæ illustrentur & ornentur . Ac meum quidem consilium tibi probatum iri confido , munusq; hoc te qua semper consueuisti humanitate accepturum, quod certè ab animo tui obseruantissimo proficiscitur , tibiq; defertur . Reliquum est ut nos diligas , & quando tam alacri animo patrocinium literarum suscepisti , librum hunc ab obtrectatorum maledictis defendes atque tuebere . Vale.

div.p: NTONIVS Posseuinus, iuuenis cum morum suauitate & elegantia, tum etiam eruditione incredibili, hosce Lælij Capilu- pi Centones miro artificio è Virgilianis uersibus concinnatos, ab auctore quotidia- nis propè conuicijs extortos ediderat. Cum autem Lælius pro singulari sua in uiros bonarum artium & literarum stu- diosos beneuolentia, nonnulla mihi illorum exemplaria litte- ratis arbitratu meo condonanda dedisset: Benedictum Ae- gium Spoletinũ, qui quanta sit doctrina, & humanitate præ- ditus, neminem latere existimo, tanto munere non indignum esse censui. Is uerò ubi id operis perlegit, supraeditum disti- cum huic argumento accommodatum conscripsit, mihíq; le- gendum dedit: quod cum ego memoriæ mandassem, paulo post Capilupo obuiam factus, recitaui. Qui statim pro disti- cho, ut est memoriæ, iudicij, sapientiæ, & liberalitatis exi- miæ, feracissimam terram imitatus, solidum Centonem in B. Aegij laudem uel sesquihoræ spatio composuit. Quocircà ope reprætium me facturum arbitratus, uolens libensq; pro An- tonio Posseuino mei longè omnium amantissimo, cui, quòd, abe

rat,id reliquum conficere non licebat , extrema hac pagella hunc quoq; Centonem, ut duorũ simul amicorũ immortalita ti hac etiam in parte consuleretur , ijsdem typis impressum appingendum curaui. ¶ Vale.
Centos out of Virgil, by Laelius Capilupi, patrician of Mantua.

Of all those whatsoever who bring something forth into the light, there are two kinds: the one comprising those by whom the matters themselves are invented, the other comprising those who take up elsewhere what they mean to say. And this latter kind is in turn divided into two parts: for either they take material from others and set it forth in their own words, or they transfer and adapt the words of others to their own purposes — which indeed applies to those who compose Centos. In this genre Lelio Capilupi was so remarkable that he easily surpassed and exceeded everyone's expectation. For although he deals for the most part with matters most remote from the age of the ancients, he nevertheless treats and encompasses them by means of Virgil's verses so skillfully that I do not think even the Poet himself could have done better. For both in the arrangement and order of the thoughts, and in joining together and, as it were, cementing the verses — which in Virgil's own books are separated from one another by the greatest distance — he has achieved this, in the judgment of all, that the work seems rather a continuous and unbroken composition than one gathered and assembled from every quarter. In this I am often accustomed to admire that man's memory and keen judgment, who could gather matters so scattered into a single place and arrange them in such a way that the middle answers to the beginning, and the beginning to the end. And just as a consummate craftsman, who out of the most varied stones fashions an outstanding work and composes it as a mosaic, so he, out of all the passages of Virgil, culled and gathered whatever was best and most suited above all to his own purpose, and from them fashioned this one body of work. I know, moreover, that a number of others have applied themselves to this kind of writing; among their number, among the Greeks, was

Eudocia, and among the Latins Proba Falconia and Ausonius — but how far they succeeded in this, let others judge. This much, indeed, I would affirm without hesitation: that in this respect they were not only not superior to Laelius, but perhaps scarcely even his equals. For, to speak of Ausonius, since he was dealing with the very subject matter itself, it was easy for him to fit the Poet's verses to what he meant; for a far different sense is imposed upon these writings than that which underlies the Virgilian lines themselves.

Since, then, I had read these Centos very often, and foresaw that this book, if published, would be most delightful and most useful to everyone, I asked Laelius to grant me leave to bring it out; and when he, as is his custom, most courteously permitted me this, nothing was dearer to me or more pressing than that it should come into men's hands. For besides the very great and abundant benefit that anyone at all would derive from it, I knew that I myself would gain no small advantage; nor indeed could anything sweeter or more pleasant befall me than that the writings of that man should be brought forth — a man to whom, quite apart from the fact that I am joined to him by the closest ties of goodwill and friendship, [omitted: struck-through word, illegible] I have always been devoted with the deepest love, not only on account of our shared love of our homeland, which he shares with many others, but also on account of his singular virtues. Moreover, I saw that this would be of the greatest use to me, since by this occasion I might open a way of approach to you, and in some measure court your favor. For you are one who, endowed with the highest virtue and most accomplished in every literary pursuit, so admired the writings of Laelius Capilupi that, although you did not even know the man by sight, you nevertheless loved and cherished him wonderfully — a thing owed both to his genius and to your own courtesy and disposition inclined toward learning. So great is the power that shared pursuits have over human minds, that the more liberal they are, the more they bind and constrain men to one another by certain ties. Moved by these considerations, I resolved to send this book to you, since I knew that with no one could it find a better or more honorable place. For as you have always spent your leisure and your time in learning, so too [you have always been devoted] to that most eminent Cardinal—

...are joined by blood — a man in whom one could not easily judge whether his character was made illustrious and adorned by his learning, or his learning by his character. And for my part, I trust that my design will meet with your approval, and that you will receive this gift with the courtesy you have always shown, since it proceeds, certainly, from a mind most devoted to you, and is offered to you. It remains only that you love us, and — since you have taken up the patronage of letters with such a ready spirit — that you will defend and protect this book from the slanders of its detractors. Farewell.

O glory, O deservedly the greatest part of our fame,

Break off delays: a way must be tried, by which I too might be able

Nymphs, our delight, present deities, Fauns,

From here I shall begin to sing. When Gallus was perishing of love,
what groves, or what glades held you, girls [Naiads]?
Pan, the god of Arcadia, came, whom we ourselves saw,
the shepherd came too; the slow swineherds came,
and a race of men born of tree-trunks and hard oak,

The sheep stand around, and with frequent lowings the rivers
and dry banks resound. Lying beneath a crag,
alas, pitiable boy, all profess that they know;

just as the nightingale, mourning beneath the poplar's shade,

lg.l: and the mother calls both the gods and the stars cruel,

By chance, one day, where huge, with slow windings, it wanders,
the Mincius, his horns gilded upon a bull-like face,
among the poplar leaves, and the resounding groves,
while he sings, and the Muse consoles his sorrowful love:
far off, in the middle of the wood, she came to meet him,
the cause of so great an evil, most beautiful Deiopea,
whose quiver sounds from her shoulder—the bow and arms of Diana—
just as a gem gleams, her hair is bound up in gold,
a golden brooch fastens her purple gown.
The youth recognized the marks of divine beauty;
a strange numbness loosened his limbs with fear;
he was struck dumb at the first sight, and his voice stuck in his throat;
as soon as he could speak, thus he began:
sighing, and drawing his voice from the depths of his breast:
"Dear offspring of the gods, most welcome to my heart,
hail, true offspring of Jove, my greatest care,
whom neither length of days nor any devotion softens,
will you alone waste away, grieving, in perpetual youth,
already ripe for a husband? And will you never know the rewards of Venus?
Ah, unhappy maiden, cast this care from your breast;
make use of your lot, and do not trust too much in your beauty;
age carries off all things, irretrievable time flees."
"Kindly one, I beg, have mercy on a spirit bearing things it does not deserve,

Scarcely had he spoken these words: just as if someone had stained
ivory with purple, such colors the maiden showed upon her face:
she cast down her gaze, and spoke with lowered voice:
"Cease to inflame both me and yourself with your complaints;
the care which you bear for my sake, this, I beg, best one, for my sake
set aside — I who have so often already disdained suitors;
my mind remains unmoved, content with Diana alone;
for — I will confess it — I do not seek the joys of life;
it is resolved, in the woods, amid the wild beasts' deserted haunts,
I am resolved to prefer to endure. Lay aside the frenzy you have begun in vain.
"Learn, boy, virtue from me, and not to scorn the gods;
This is the reward of piety. The gate of black Dis stands open;
Minos, the inquisitor, examines lives and crimes,
and chastises, and hears out deceits: a grim [reckoning] awaits you,
a punishment, and too late, with prayers, you will worship the gods."
So she speaks, and with her words breathes divine love [into him],
she teaches him what trust may be placed in human affairs —
Love disturbs him all the more, and he sickens from the very curing of it.
Then, shaking his head, he poured out these words from his breast:
"I have understood everything, and already gone through it beforehand in my mind;
do not fashion such great fears for me: such things are no concern of his;
Love conquers all, and the roar of greedy Acheron
he has cast beneath his feet: for what measure could there be to Love?
Thence the race of men and of cattle, and the painted birds,
and the race of the sea, seek the seeds of generation,
they rush into frenzy and fire. The priestess-queen,
heavy with Mars [pregnant by him], brought forth in travail into the light
the Romans, lords of the world and the toga-clad race.
Why should I pursue greater things? Boys, and unwed girls
ascended the unwelcome couch of great-hearted Jove.
And do men hesitate to take up Nature's tasks?
Laurentine nymphs, nymphs of surpassing bodily beauty,
to live after the manner of a wild beast — what madness has driven you [to this]?
vain superstition, to have worshipped Diana amid the thickets,
an eternal love of weapons and of virginity:
splendid praise indeed, and ample spoils you bring back —
after the cost of such great efforts, for all that nothing has been accomplished.
Will you suffer so many labors to have been spent in vain?
Rather take pity: you will finally force me to die.
Receive my pledge, and give yours in turn; since we two have come together,
Do you wish, then, that between us what each of us in turn can do
let us try?
Nor am I so ill-formed. You alone [I hold] worthy of the maiden,
and Phoebus loves me too; for the seer knows all things,
the whole grove shall sing of you; if my songs can do anything,
your honor, and your name, and your praises shall ever remain,
if no glory of such great things moves you,
turn now both your eyes hither, look upon our affairs.
Open now Helicon, goddesses, and set your songs in motion.
A monstrous weapon, which by chance he carried in his strong hand,
he took it away while soothing him—than which nothing more excellent [is held by]
in Europe and Asia—a portent wondrous to behold—
horrible, with a misshapen head and a monstrous mass of neck,
a covering interwoven with thorns, and a long beard,
and dewlaps hang down from the chin as far as the legs;
so enormous was its bulk. Am I to entrust myself to this monster?
Having spoken these things, she falls silent, and pours forth tears, and fills the whole
place with her cry, and, trembling, flees back,
like one who unexpectedly, among rough brambles, has stepped upon a snake
on the ground and, with a cry, has drawn his foot back,
but he pursued her alike with speed and spear,

lg.l: “Halt! Where are you rushing now, where are you hurrying away?” he said.
You shall not escape today; I shall come through weapons and through fire.
there are no snares here; I swear by earth, sea, and stars.
Weapons have no force; as she bends back her smooth neck,
he pursues her, now—now!—has her in his grasp, and bears upon her with his spear.
The unhappy [maiden] flies forth, and with womanly wailing,
her hair torn, fills the region far and wide with mournful laments.
All-powerful Fortune, what may we lovers not hope for?
Here the youth, already exulting in victory, on the trampled ground
could not keep his staggering footing; he rolled back upon the sand
the unlucky one slips, not forgetful of his loves;
he groaned, and gave forth these words from the depths of his breast:
Only be at hand, you who scorn the bolts of Typhoeus,
be kindly and propitious; favor my bold undertaking.
Son of a goddess, if ancient piety has any regard for human sufferings,
do not fail me in these desperate circumstances.
we have come to the last extremity; if you are moved by any prayers,
come now, and draw forth the avenging arrow from the quiver."
Scarcely had he uttered this, when suddenly all things seemed to collapse,
Love obeys the words; in the serene region of the sky
Thunder sounded on the left; at once the death-bringing bow rang out.
he took his stand here, and with the curved horn [of the bow] aimed the shafts;
Unseen by anyone, the arrow sped through her flank
and it was fixed in the left side — wondrous to tell —
it pervades her senses and entwines fire within her bones.
Shameless Love, to what god has such great power been granted?
I do not indeed envy — I marvel the more. The fierce maiden,
checked her step, and, suddenly kindled with frenzy,
begins to speak out: "We follow you, holy one of the gods,
whoever you are: behold, a suppliant I come, have mercy on your own,"
she cries: “Io, glory, and Latonian guardian of the groves,
gods and goddesses all, whose care it is to watch over the fields,
“Here,” he said, “is your home. Farewell now, woods.”
A greater god drives me on and sends me back to greater tasks.
Love came, and stirred my heart with a sudden sweetness.
You indeed, boy worthy of reverence, I receive and acknowledge with all my heart,
since this concern gnaws at you.
come hither, O beautiful boy; now is the time to act:
I grant what you wish, but this unfamiliar business troubles our minds.
whatever it is, I fear it: I beg you, ward off this frenzy.
Having heard these things, he made this reply with a calm face.
I call the gods to witness, dear one: nothing sorrowful will follow once he is received;
take him by the hand, for he will follow willingly and readily.
Fortune favors the bold: who but a madman would refuse
such things? And he confirms her resolve with a present pledge.
At these words their cares were dispelled: the venerable gift
of the fateful wand, a memorial and a pledge of love —
she indeed, with sweet allurements, a wanton girl,
she marvels at it and turns it over in her hands and arms,
she cannot satisfy her mind, and grows inflamed by gazing.
Then indeed he caught fire, and desire rose erect in the youth;
the skin, hard to the touch, resists the hand that handles it;
the unseemly limbs, stirred, begin to swell,
spirit animates it within and, diffused through its limbs, the whole
the mind stirs the mass: rising, it lifts its head higher;
he, submitting to her hand and rejoicing in so great an honor,
cannot stand still in one place; he burns, ardent with sudden hope,
exulting with joy, and lashes the air with blows.
She, for her part, [the shafts] long since drawn on the ready bow,
holding her shafts, prays thus to the Moon on high:
“If I rightly remember the tale, Pan, god of Arcadia,
lured you, Moon, captive into the deep woods and deceived you.”
You who are no stranger to suffering, come to the aid of our undertaking.
When she had spoken these words: “May the gods prosper our undertakings —
At last, rejoicing, he said: “What worthy thanks shall I be able to render,
I who shall never forget so great a service?
O glory of Italy, while life rules these limbs,
always with my honor, always shall you be celebrated with gifts."
She approaches, her shining eyes suffused with tears:
"say no more, boy, and let us do what now presses upon us;
break every delay: woman is always fickle and changeable.
By it she calms the sky and the storms,
she soothes him, hesitant, in a soft embrace. Suddenly he says,
“This is what I so often sought in my prayers.”
Having said this, he threw back the double cloak from his shoulders;
Eagerly he tore apart the knots and linen fastenings;
beside a stream of water he lies down on the green sedge;
as she opened the folds of her dress and beckoned with all her garment,
he seizes her, locks her in a knotted embrace, and clings close, crushing her.
brandishing the monstrous weapon in his hand, he bursts through every barrier,
joining hand to hand and mouth to mouth,
breast to breast. Boys and unwed maidens,
take flight! Away, away, you profane—be gone!
I set in motion a greater work. [Their] legs, the buskins stripped away,
they say [the legs] sprang apart: the doors torn away, the dark house
it opens: and Cacus's [den], laid bare, appeared, huge —
the palace, and gave forth a huge window with a wide opening
of its own accord: the shadowy caverns lay open deep within.
Here was that labor of the house, and its inextricable maze;
here was a cave, monstrous with a vast gaping mouth,
bristling, which dense brambles had filled on every side;
within, sweet waters, and honey's heavenly gifts.
In the very forecourt, and in the first jaws of Orcus,

lg.l: there was a circle, celebrated by fame in many lands,
sacred far and wide by the religion of our fathers: on every side hills,
hollow, enclosed it — memorials of unspeakable love.
Behold, raging in spirit, and turned about with a horsehair bowstring,
that shameless boy — [there,] where a narrow path leads,
and narrow throats, and grudging approaches, lead on,
he grazes along his path, and fixes the bough upon the opposing threshold.
(May the gods grant better things to the pious, and turn that error upon our enemies!)
I shudder as I tell it. She stood, transfixed with sharp grief,
rolling her eyes this way and that, and casts, in turn,
impatient of the wound, with breast raised, her legs,
driven by heavy frenzy. "What of me? What cause has driven [you]
along an unaccustomed path? I shall lead you by a broad track;
this is the way. Indeed I feared nothing of the kind concerning you:"
"Gallus, why do you rave?" Blood follows from the wound.
"Why," he said, "do you go off on a different way? The path deceives those going [along it]:"
to this he [replies]: teach me the way, and open the sacred doors.
But the hero, not slowed by mischance, nor terrified,
unwinding the whole tangled path of the deceptive wood,
hissing, it passes through the middle of his thigh, and thus he speaks:
"I have found, sister, a way: let all fear be gone,
I go forward, having dared to unlock the sacred springs,
let us hasten," he says. What [rites], duly begun, I have prepared
it is my intent to complete, and to set an end to [my] cares.
So they carry through the journey they had begun, and press kisses
joyful with I know not what sweetness beyond the usual,
with quivering tongues they licked [their] hissing jaws,
and forthwith, when the flame had been set beneath the eager marrow,
the same ardor drives them all at once, and equally the task,
having shared it by lot: the moisture, warmed in the tender bones,
seethes; and they distend the cells with liquid nectar.
Then indeed [his] eyes blazed, and, drawn from deep within,
a heavier breath is heard: and, drawn out, they murmur
with a groan: suddenly neither face nor color stayed the same.
Her combed hair did not stay in place. The girl, about to die,
rolling a bloodshot gaze, and with quivering spots
spread over her cheeks, tasting kisses, speaks:
"O, if Jupiter would but bring back to me my bygone years,
while you, dear boy, my only and late delight,
I hold in my embrace — with you might I be consumed through all my life;
now I know what love is — my own blood.
This she said, and poured forth the liquid fragrance of ambrosia,
and to her the hero thus gave answer in few words:
"You have destroyed yourself, and me too, sister." And, saying no more,
gnashing his teeth, rolling his flaming eyes,
and from this side and that, he unwound its monstrous coils,
and stirs up its final groans: then the gleaming serpent
collapses, and vomits from its mouth blood mixed with foam.
Ah me, what he once was, how changed from that [former self];
he laid down his bent neck, and lay stretched through the cave;
and he furrows his foul brow with wrinkles: all, and at once,
his warmth slipped away, and a foul sweat, [his limbs] reeking,
followed over his limbs: and, this being done, here he grew still.
Cease the Maenalian verses, now cease, O flute;
it shall be enough, goddesses, that your poet has sung these things,
while he sits, and the sheep graze, and the eager heifers,
Pierides, you shall make this the greatest thing for Gallus.

div.note: The falling verse signifies strength failing during intercourse (impotence).

lg.l: I am he who once, when GALLUS was perishing with love,
night and day I sang beneath the covering of the beech-tree.
With ancestral songs, [I sing] the spectacles of trifling matters,
I set in motion a greater work: not here with feigned song
great-souled AENEAS, [do I sing], nor you, lacking reason,
unhappy Dido, after the death of wretched Sychaeus:
but the BROTHERS -- masters of the world, and the toga-clad race --
illustrious souls, and hearts forgetful of toils,
I shall indeed speak, relying on the lyre and the tuneful strings,
of fate-telling Manto: we cannot all do all things,
O glory of Italy, distinguished in piety and in arms,
care of the gods, Hippolytus, offspring most beautiful in war,
led through so many men from the origin of the ancient race;
Whether you, for me, now surmount the cold of great Rhine,
bristling with javelins, and in the hide of a Libyan she-bear,
amid the arms of kings, and on your shield, as the paternal device,
you bear a hundred snakes, and wear a hydra girt about with serpents,
towering, rising up, and shaking great lilies,
or on the banks of the Po, to the august walls of the king,
whence you draw your lineage, conspicuous in Tyrian purple,
amid the sacred rites of the gods you give laws to the fathers summoned:
grant an easy course, and favor bold undertakings.
from Jove the beginning of the race (if it be worthy to believe),
although born of gods, now with so many years slipping by --

lg.l: a monster horrible, shapeless, huge, from which the light [of sight] was taken away.
even father Pluto himself hates it; her sisters [the Furies] hate it;
small from fear at first, soon it lifts itself into the air,
as tenacious of the false and the depraved, as it is a messenger of the true:
and day by day, rising, it lifts its greedy head higher.
what region on earth is not full of our toil?
behold too the world subdued by farmers at its furthest reaches,
and the Britons, utterly cut off from the whole world.
why should I recount the unspeakable slaughters, and forbidden marriages?
all dared a monstrous crime, and achieved what they had dared.
they seized the sacred image, and with bloody hands
they tore apart the altars, and the sacred [precincts] of the gods --
the thresholds: everywhere terror, and the image of death in many a form.
indeed, having rampaged through the midst of the cities of Italy,
a plague, and the wrath of the gods, having begun a greater madness --
I speak of things not unknown: all confess that they know it.
he indeed, he, Asylas, interpreter of men and of gods,
in face and shoulders like a god, on whose chin very much
unkempt hoariness lies, [and] his mantle hangs down,
squalid, from his shoulders; whom every age believed [descended]
from ethereal seed, and a lineage from the high blood of the gods,
he breaks off every law, and, trembling, suddenly flees back,
his tunics embroidered with the needle; into so many faces he turns himself,
ah me, what he once was, how changed from that former self,
powerful in sedition, and trained also in Greek cunning,
he went, and bore himself along with a mighty shout,
having entered upon the turning of tricks by counsel, and by cunning,
he filled the peoples of fertile Ausonia [Italy] with talk,
forgetful of his own honor, and of the safety of his companions,
having dared, moreover, to tear away from the consecrated temple
the great divinities of the gods.

div.note: By 'the safety of his companions' he means the monks of that order, whom Bernardino, by his flight, brought into disrepute.

lg.l: And the tunics have sleeves, and the mitres have ribbons,
but the immortal race, having followed the precepts of God,
they toil to mend the ruins of a fallen lineage.
the fortune of the house stands firm, and grandsires of grandsires are counted,
they choose laws and magistrates, and a sacred senate,
governors of the young, and of affairs, and a dread king,
and those whom they prefer to devote to the keeping of livestock,
while the minds of the young are pliant, while their age is changeable,
or to reserve for the sacred altars, or to plough the earth --
another hoards wealth; to the aged the towns are a care;
there are some to whom guard-duty at the gates has fallen by lot;
on all, in the customary manner, the hair is shorn, and their backs are fat,
and dewlaps hang down from the chin as far as the legs,
all have the same purpose: to swell themselves out with thick fat --
whom they have chosen as leader; but the lineage is not the same for all;
but neither how many the kinds are, nor what the names are,
is there a number; for indeed I could not run through the names,
not if I had a hundred tongues, and a hundred mouths,
his own day stands fixed for each: brief, and irretrievable, is the time
allotted to all: an age will come, as the lustres glide by,
when the house, and all the offspring, shall suddenly fail.
alas, it is right for no one to trust, the gods being unwilling.
what do labor or good deeds avail? Thus all things by the fates
rush toward the worse, and, slipping back, are carried backward.
then let him know [it]: if anyone [would behold] the airy Alps and the Norican,
let him see the strongholds on the hills, and the deserted kingdoms,
here once, from a sickness of the sky, there arose, pitiable to see,
a vain superstition, ignorant also of the ancient gods,
which it is right for no one to lay low, neither by fire nor by the sword.
customs, and pursuits, and peoples, dwellings held in common --
this earlier [plague], sent forth from Stygian darkness, did away with [them].
driven by the fates, they wandered around all the seas;
no one had a fixed home: they dwelt in the lowest valleys,
a secluded grove, and a cave beneath overhanging crags,
and the grassy banks of rivers, amid the wastes of wild beasts,
beneath the burning sun, and beneath the icy pole of the sky.
even then religion terrified the fearful country-folk;
a wretched sustenance -- berries, and stony cornel-cherries --
the branches give, and the grasses feed them with plucked-up roots.
their cups are the clear springs. Not the Massic gifts
of Bacchus [wine]; nor did banquets set out again and again harm them;
no Venus, nor did any marriage-rites bend their spirit?
alas, piety, alas, ancient faith -- who, in telling of such things,
could restrain himself from tears? After a long time there came
the one [being] who, for us, [was] a God sent from high heaven;
he tamed the untaught race, scattered on the high mountains,
and gave them laws; to seek new dwellings
the same ardor drives them all at once. Toil conquered all things,
relentless [toil], and want that presses hard in difficult circumstances.
great-hearted heroes, born in better years,
in Europe and Asia, and beyond the Garamantes and the Indians,
they inhabit a hundred great cities, and golden dwellings,
golden now, once bristling with woodland brambles:
so much can length of distant age avail to change [things] --
now also to endure poverty, and hard toils,
through rocks, and crags, and the love of virginity,
religion forbade [it], by the warning and command of the gods;
what am I saying? Or does dread desire become for each man a god?
therefore with every zeal, joyful, they attend to their feasts
before the hearth, if it be cold, [or] in the shade, if it be harvest,
this is the work of virtue; lest the cold ice should harm
the soft flock, and bring the mange, and shameful gout.

lg.l: therefore all Etruria rose up in righteous fury;
then to hasten flight: he unearths from the ground the old
treasures, an unknown weight of silver and of gold,
conscious of the bold deed, he made his way to the cities,
and the hateful race, and the shrines of dread Dis,
fleeing the arms of Jove, and the walls of lofty Rome.
and now that Paris, with his half-male retinue,
where the fire [is] in the middle, and companions wreathe the mixing-bowl,
pouring libation to you, Lenaean [Bacchus], calls out, lying on his back in the cave,
the cause of so great an evil, a garment gleaming with purple dye --
unhappy Envy, and the boundless desire for praise,
nowhere is trust safe -- a SERPENT that has fed on evil herbs
an instigator of crimes, drove [him] on with bitter goads,
for indeed he did not rest, until from the topmost roof-ridge
amid the rocks he thrust the man down to the Stygian waters.
as an unfed lion, often roaming the lofty stalls,
now these, now those approaches, and wanders through the whole
of Italy, Italy, it turns its winding coils,
and bristles with raised scales, and hisses with its mouth --
I shudder as I recount it: Gods, avert such a mischance;
Gods, forbid the threats: only let Mantua survive for us,
Mantua, rich in ancestors, like the Berecynthian mother [Cybele],
joyful in her divine offspring: far off, oh far off, be gone, you profane ones --
ancestral gods, preserve the household, and the small grandsons,
and, being gracious, preserve the pious, and the powerful mistress.
you I beseech, Alcides [Hercules], great and memorable divinity,
whom we worship first, [you who are] pitying our misfortunes:
protect first this house, the fierce race of WOLVES;
in this may the grandsons remain chaste, in this religion,
and the sons of sons, and those who shall be born from them.
where am I carried? Whence have I departed? Irretrievable time flees,

lg.l: while, captivated by love, we survey each thing one by one:
and besides I leave behind many things to be recorded after me.
you, O Calliope, I pray, breathe favor upon me as I sing,
the rites, and the gods, the feasts, and the cups of the full table,
the brave deeds of the FATHERS. Now must it be sounded with a great voice --
every race indeed on earth, the people, and the FATHERS,
from soft bedding, kindly light rouses [them] to their work,
and the morning song of birds beneath the roof-ridge.
at the outset they approach the shrines, and with resounding bronze,
either on high towers, or on the ridge of the highest roof,
they give the signal, and suddenly the whole sky thunders with a crash;
then at last, creaking on their dread-sounding hinge, the sacred
doors are thrown open; fearful mothers in long line,
and feeble old men, boys, and unmarried girls
have left their homes; around the kindled altars,
gathered from every side, joyful, [each with] whatever store he has,
they bring gifts, and load the altars, and press kisses [upon them],
and they implore all the gods who hold the heights above,
and now the priests, who alone are skilled in singing,
veiled in linen, flit about, resplendent too in purple,
and equally matched in singing, and ready to respond,
they gleam in a divided company, and circle round in dances.
the halls; lamps hang down from the golden fretted ceilings,
altars stand around: and the priest, in pure vestment,
thunders forth three hundred gods from his mouth; three times from his throat, his voice
or four times redouble; then the rest of the youth follows,
and hear our prayers: and in the temples the priest,
before the altars, a suppliant, venerates with a full incense-casket,
and addresses the gods, stretching his palms to the stars,
he cries out that he is the cause, the crime, and the source of the evils,
and accuses himself of much, and with a swift mouth added these words:

lg.l: hail, holy parent, ruler of high Olympus.
forever shall your honor and name, and your praises, remain,
approach favorably both us and your rites with propitious foot,
we, your offspring, to whom you grant the citadel of heaven --
these feasts, as is the custom (he left these memorials
now in his last death) -- this altar of so great a divinity
we build, having been saved, and we renew the deserved honors.
Son of the highest Father, is it not through these wounds of yours that I am kept safe,
living [because] of your death? What unworthy cause has defiled
your serene countenance, or why do I see these wounds?
piety conquered the hard journey: you the gatekeeper of Orcus --
the Stygian pools trembled at you: you [won over] the scepter, and Jove,
you reconcile: you grant [us] to recline at the feasts of the gods,
spare the pious race, and look more closely upon our affairs,
all gods and goddesses; and you, O most holy prophetess,
kindly parent, come present to the aid of our toil.
when he had spoken these words from his divine mouth, the priest
the gifts of laboured Ceres [bread], celestial gifts,
marvels at, and turns them between his hands and his arms;
alas, what is he to do? confounded by the varied image of things,
and now this way, now that way, he swiftly divides his mind,
and drags it into various directions, when to turn his bites
toward the scanty Ceres [bread] the gods, by their divine will, urged [him],
to violate too with his hand, and with bold jaws, the round [loaf],
of the fateful crust; he struck his honest breast
three and four times with his hand; he gives a groan from the depth of his breast;
thus he speaks: 'I do not indeed deem myself worthy of such an honor' --
and a sacred cup filled his right hand: swiftly all
lowered their heads, the mothers, their breasts smitten;
the elders recognized the god: he, undaunted, drained
the foaming bowl, and washed himself down with the full [cup of] gold.

lg.l: 'Go,' he says, and carried the pure water around to his companions,
sprinkling with a light dew, and left the altars stripped of offerings.
without delay, straightway, the vows having been duly completed in order,
the elder rises up, and called the gods to witness the vows,
his head bared, and, standing in the middle on the mound, he speaks,
harsh, sounding bitter things, alone amid all who listen intently,
he sings of the fates, his beard spread combed down upon his breast;
he teaches what trust is to be placed in human affairs --
the jaws of Tartarus too, and the profound night,
and the brothers sworn together to tear open heaven,
the punishments and penalties for crimes, and the blessed abodes,
the juices of ambrosia, and the fragrant panacea [cure-all herb].
he warns, and mingles prayers, and casts forth alternately
his arms outstretched, rolling his flaming eyes;
he holds his face fixed in a gaze, and stands motionless on the ground,
he begins to speak, and stops in the middle of his utterance,
he transforms himself into all manner of wondrous shapes,
he, bringing thirst and diseases to sick mortals,
sings dread riddles, and, present, threatens
destruction, turning over the records of ancient men,
heats and rains, and the winds that drive the cold,
and foul famine, and announces grim wraths.
the hearts of the farmers shudder; the unknowing crowd stands amazed;
the mothers, out of fear, double their vows, and, driven by frenzy,
cry out together; the halls resound far and wide with lamentations,
with wailings, and groaning, and womanly ululation.
shouting such things, he raises himself up from his lofty throne,
his temples still bare, and he is clothed in a tunic about his limbs;
then he takes up his wand: with this he calls forth souls from Orcus;
around him countless peoples, a pitiable crowd,
and after him, other chiefs: and he learns their lives and their crimes,

lg.l: bearing gifts, and talents of ivory and of gold,
bristly swine, and Dodonaean cauldrons,
he escorts [them] with pardon, and addresses [them] with friendly words,
[them] now exhausted by every mischance, in need of everything,
he chastises, and hears [them], and sends [them] to impious Tartarus.
but those who alone brooded over wealth [once] found,
cast down by a thunderbolt, are rolled in the lowest depth.
and while these things are being carried on in an utterly different quarter,
a stately dwelling, huge, raised aloft on a hundred columns,
is being fitted out, and in the midst of the halls they prepare a banquet.
some set the bronze cauldrons in order, and tend the flames,
some [heat] the hot waters, and fix quivering [meats] on the spits --
the chines of swine, a hundred fat lambs with their dams,
some load the tables with dishes, and Ceres [bread] in baskets
they set out, and bring napkins of shorn nap.
others place the knives beneath, and serve Bacchus [wine];
they run about, and take turns in shifts; and, the altars left behind,
the FATHERS, accustomed to sit at continuous tables,
murmur around the CLOISTER, and stand with ears pricked up;
attentively they await the signal, and pray to the gods.
then the almighty FATHER, to whom belongs the highest power over affairs,
comes forth at last, with a great throng attending him --
a monster horrible, huge, its body swollen thick with mixed fodder;
in the manner of the FATHERS, he sat down in the midst on the ancestral throne,
he, the guardian of the works: him they admire, and all
stand around him with a dense murmur; as often has arisen
sedition, and discord rages, driving on the BROTHERS,
he rules their spirits with his words; and the proud brothers
he restrains by his command, and curbs with chains and prison.
'Not so, boys; do not grow accustomed in your hearts to such great wars,
and you, PRIOR, you spare [them], you who derive your lineage from Olympus.'

The head of the monks is called the Prior.

lg.l: these things having been observed, first amid such works
of his own accord he raises their spirits with words, and rebukes them unprompted:
'O comrades -- for indeed we are not unacquainted with former ills --
this was that hunger; this final trial awaited us,
through various mischances, through so many crises of affairs,
[it] was to set a limit to our ruin. Now there is need of strength,
now of swift hands, now of every masterly skill;
what you have longed for in your prayers is at hand: thus one goes to the stars.
come then, and all of you, now put forth those powers,
and call upon the god common [to us all], and pour out wine willingly.'
this was the end of his speech; and from the throne he made the whip resound,
and when the signal was given, each withdrew to his own place
(all things in their proper order); then silence fell upon their tongues,
thus was frenzy added to the spirits of the young men: then, like wolves,
plunderers in the black mist, they snatch and rush about,
and they tear apart the food, and by their touch defile everything;
no delay, no rest: with utmost rivalry they
strip the hides from the ribs; then with tenacious tooth
they make their din; their jaws crackle under the harsh wound;
they are filled with old wine, and with fat game;
in the Teutonic fashion they drain the bronze mixing-bowls dry.
after hunger was banished by the feast, one voice rose from all --
to pay worthy thanks to the king of the heaven-dwellers
is not within our power. In the midst of such words
joyful with some sweetness beyond the usual, I know not what,
they came down to joyful places, and gave themselves over to song,
as once, snow-white swans amid the clear clouds,
when they betake themselves back from feeding: here, around the rivers,
the ground pours forth flowers; vines weave shady bowers;
here [are] cool springs, and meadows fresh with streams,
caves, and living pools, and the lairs of wild beasts.

div.note: Grace after the meal (thanksgiving after dinner).

lg.l: then to catch wild beasts with snares, and to deceive [birds] with birdlime --
they devote their care, and to set nets for stags,
and to chase long-eared hares; and in the river's channel,
when the winds have fallen, another draws in wet nets;
some exercise their limbs in grassy wrestling-grounds
and tear their thin TUNICS, through the shadowy parts of the roads;
some beat out dances with their feet, and recite songs;
the whole grove resounds with the din, and with unrestrained laughter.
then, if by chance they [catch sight of] some man weighty in piety and in merits,
once they have caught sight of him, they fall silent, or, having turned, gave their backs [fled];
but the youth, patient of toil, and accustomed to little,
either take up the burdens of those arriving, or, forming a column,
a way is made by force, they penetrate the halls, and the thresholds of kings;
others run about to the gates, and to the roofs of the houses;
it delights them to haul together plunder, and to live by rapine;
and, mindful of the coming winter, they store up what they have sought,
or the offspring of sheep, or goats grazing on the cultivated fields;
chestnuts too, and, likewise, the grain crops follow,
meanwhile the priest calls his companions into the lofty temples,
long since idle: and the youth, poured forth from the fields,
gather together from every side, and conduct sorrowful funerals,
lest anything be left untried, following the clashing bronze [cymbals];
then twin brothers, whose age does not differ much,
seized the funeral torches, according to ancient custom;
boys walk in procession, and bodies, having finished with life,
(what race of men is this) they carry back joyfully with a shout;
here [are] wretched mothers, and boys bereft of their parents,
they weep in sorrow; the sky resounds with great lamentations,
and the earth is sprinkled with tears, and the soft bier
they themselves cast up joyful cries to the stars,
through the midst of the cities: the priest, with his long robe,

div.note: The monks' inner garments are called 'tunics'.

lg.l: and purified the men, and spoke his last words
to the shades and the ashes, [praying] how softly the bones may rest,
then chosen young men, in the middle vault of the temple
rush in, close-packed, and strip the still-warm limbs.
by the religion of the fathers, and they learn to hide [them] away in pits.
meanwhile evening draws nearer, as heaven slopes down;
they seek their dwellings; late in the night the MINORS betake themselves home,
they renew the feast, and the welcome gifts of the second table
they bring; torches conquer the night with their flames;
they rolled elm-logs to the hearths, and gave them to the fire,
the genial winter invites, and dissolves their cares;
then [come] sweet sleep, and then the softest wines.
after the first repose from feasting, and the tables removed,
under the long porticoes, [young men] needing no great praise,
and feeble old men, buried in sleep and in wine,
fell silent; sleep enfolds their weary limbs.
for all there is one rest from toil; for all, one labor.
but not sluggish in [the affairs of] Venus, and in sweet stolen [pleasures],
outstanding in beauty, and youth in its earliest bloom,
defended by the darkness, and by the gift of the shadowy night,
they rush into frenzies, and into the fire; neither the CLOISTER, nor
the guards themselves are able to withstand [it]: Love is the same for all.
many besides, [with] whatever remains for their needy circumstances,
often with their own hand distend the CELLS with flowing nectar.
joys thrill through the breast of the great-hearted heroes,
and a poison, the solace of their ill, drips from the groin.
O too fortunate, if they but knew their own blessings:
they do not lack woodland pastures, and joyful herds,
there are many talents of chased silver and of gold,
the sacred rites of the gods, and the holy FATHERS; and the dear [hearts] of the SISTERS,
the breasts of those who mourn, in darkness and in blind confinement.

div.note: Monks devoted to St. Francis, whom they call the Minorites (Friars Minor).

lg.l: a hundred bronze bolts shut it; and often, without any
couplings, made pregnant by the wind -- wondrous to tell --
hallowed by religion; not these things without the divine will of the gods,
now a new race is sent down from high heaven;
I believe indeed, nor is it an empty belief, that theirs is the race of the gods.
hail, true offspring of Jove: to you a thousand names,
rich in wealth, rich in embroidered raiment, and in gold,
having embraced all the heaven-dwellers, a hundred grandsons,
hence the Italian peoples, and all the Oenotrian [Italian] land
carry away responses [from you] in doubtful matters; to you the greatest part of affairs,
and the faithfulness of words, and a life not knowing how to deceive,
[belong]; your care is to watch over the images of the gods, and the temples:
Europe, and Asia, with great tumult stirring them --
(I do not indeed grudge it) you yourself, far from discordant arms,
you will not dread the unpacified Iberians at your back;
never does care break off wholesome sleep.
and would that I had been one of you, and one of your own,
either a guardian of the flock, or a vintner of the ripe grape:
Love conquers all; for what limit could there be to Love?
he tore the breastplate together with my breast;
he drove through my ribs, and left the flying steel [lodged there];
the blade sank deeper to the quick with the wound.
what was I to do? Could I set myself against so great a monster?
O fortunate peoples, a race sprung from highest Jove --
rest is won for you; we pass the hours in weeping;
the Fates summon us hence to fresh tears and to the same dread wars; impious Mars rages over the whole world:
the fates summon; impious Mars rages over the whole world:
discord has fallen upon kings with a great upheaval;
on this side the Euphrates stirs up war, on that side Germany;
turbid, and twisting its tawny sands, the Hister [Danube],
and the Morini, farthest of mankind; so many thousand peoples --
the Italians bear arms; new blood stains the weapons.
now too portents follow, horrible to see;
foul birds of ill omen — this alone was lacking to our troubles,
and they darken the sky with their wings, and press down upon the open
fields, having become a cloud -- behold, for whom have we sown these fields?
and there is no delay for such great portents -- wars, horrid wars,
and I see the Tiber foaming with much blood.
behold, a fierce enemy, a race unconquerable in war,
victor from the peoples of the Dawn, and he threatens to cast down
the highest citadels of the Italians, and to give [them] over to destruction,
with hollow bronze, and, flying in his favoring chariot, gives the rein
through the peoples of the Greeks, and the fields of Iapidian Timavus.
alas, how great slaughters threaten the wretched Laurentines;
the extreme has been reached -- behold, to what point discord [has led] the citizens,
has it led the wretched? and Fortune has no way back.
amid these upheavals, and these such great struggles,
she herself remains unmoved, and watches the battles undismayed --
dear offspring of the gods; temples of solid marble --
she makes [them] resound with unceasing song; nor iron laws,
nor the mad forum, nor the public record-halls has it seen;
and all fears, and the din of greedy Acheron
it has cast beneath its feet, subject to no care
to await feasts, to lead solemn processions,
it delights [them] to go to the shrines, and to see the slain young bullocks --
this is their love, this their pursuit: with the utmost force of their means they strive
among royal tables, and the nymph SISTERS,
to rise into the number of the stars, and to ascend to high heaven.
this shall be the place of the city, this the sure rest from toils.
live happily, O you thrice and four times blessed,
however your fortunes shall fall, if my songs can do anything,
no day shall ever blot you from the memory of time.

div.note: He calls 'hollow bronze' the bronze engine commonly called a bombard (cannon).

lg.l: The other songs, which would have engaged idle minds,
are all now common knowledge -- what a raging Woman can do,
a race hostile to me, lovers not bound by an equal pact,
I shall indeed tell it, deceived by unworthy love for Nisa,
on whose account I was able to endure such great labors,
since otherwise I cannot exact the punishment due for [her] crime,
now, oh now, may it be granted to arm my shafts with poison,
of prophetic Manto, a great and memorable name --
it lies in the punishment of a Woman, and it will delight [me] to have glutted my spirit.
Great-hearted heroes, breathe inspiration, I pray, upon me as I sing,
keep reverent silence, all of you, and far off -- oh, far off -- be gone, ye profane,
and [thou] hated race, with [thy] half-man retinue.
And be thou present, and run through together [with me] the task begun,
O fortunate old man, great offspring of Jove,
from whom thou dost draw thy lineage, known by fame beyond the heavens,
flower of the ancients and valor of men, and priest of the gods,
in face and shoulders like unto a god, to thee [is given] abundance of speech,
generous indeed always -- rouse thy fruitful breast,
sounding no mortal sound, glide into our souls.
What things are, what have been, what soon shall come to pass --
are known to thee; now begin to grow accustomed to being called upon in vows,
if thou dost not shrink back, and art not loath to learn these slight, humble concerns,
yet soon I shall gird myself to tell of burning battles,
with thee as my guide, I shall bring back to thee, Mantua, the Idumaean palms,
I shall tell of battle-lines, and kings driven by their passions into wars,
and great-hearted leaders, and, forced entire under arms,
Europe and Asia, and the conflagrations of so great a war,
afterward the same kings, their strife laid down, among themselves
amid these upheavals, wearied in the midst of their endeavors,
meeting together they shall join right hands, and with peace as pledge
the gates of War shall be shut, and the two-horned Rhine,
turbid, and twisting its yellow sands, the Ister,
unforeseen they shall be present, in the vaulted midst of the temple --
at the Ausonian shore: with a great howling tumult,
in Teutonic fashion, before the altars, holding [libation-]bowls,
they shall give laws and statutes to men, and the rites of sacred things,
a dreadful assembly. Nor will I be silent of thee, [thou] worthy to be remembered,
with the senators and the people, the household gods and the great gods,
O Father Tiber, let them call for battle-lines, and let them join treaties;
do not thou yield to misfortunes, but go against them the more boldly,
however things may fall out, the immovable rock of the Capitol
he shall dwell beside [it], and the Roman Father shall hold empire,
sent forth into empire -- he to whom the stars of heaven are obedient,
and the flank of the underworld, and the walls of lofty Rome.
But meanwhile time flies, flies beyond recall.
Receive, therefore, into your minds, and fix fast these my words:
ye guides of youth, turn hither your joyful minds,
and the sons of sons, and those who shall be born from them.
A monster huge and dreadful, ever fickle and changeable --
WOMAN, who is most like the winds, and most like a winged dream,
thrives by her fickleness, [and] flickers with three-forked tongues from her mouth,
as tenacious of the false and the depraved as she is a messenger of the true.
she gives forth sound without sense, and from her whole burning face
sparks fly off, [and] fire flashes from her keen eyes.
alone she grieves in the empty house -- she to whom songs are ever [dear]
and the lyre are dear to her heart; fiery, with swift feet,
she flits through all places far and wide, turns over in her breast
a thousand arts of doing harm -- who could deceive a lover [like her]?
in all the temples, rejoicing in the favoring breath of the crowd,
she wears figured, embroidered robes, beneath a covering of gold,
fastening golden girdles beneath her bared breast,
and as she walks she sweeps her tracks with the end of her trailing tail,
and, her calves bound high in a purple buskin,
she paints her brow and temples with blood-red mulberries,
she draws a thousand varied colors, facing the sun,
her burning cheeks suffused [with color]; across the top of her breast there runs [the circlet],
a pliant circlet of twisted gold about her neck,
covered with gold, her locks are knotted up into tawny gold.
and [her] ambrosial locks, from the crown of her head, a divine fragrance
breathed forth; her shoulders, drenched with oil, gleam.
as a gem gleams; she turned her comely head about,
she seemed to give off burning torches -- a wonder to behold --
she parted the murky air, and scattered the shadows,
on this side and on that; so great a splendor shines from her surpassing face,
on swift wings Rumour goes through great cities:
these things the foul goddess spreads everywhere into the mouths of men.
toward her all the youth, poured forth from houses and fields,
rushes, crowding round about -- [youth] devoted to a doom to come --
gaping, with minds astonished, it gazes upon her as she passes,
nor is it enough to have seen [her] once; it delights them to linger on,
she perceived it, glad, and, for her part, not unmindful of her own art,
a plague and the wrath of the gods, rolling flaming eyes,
then to catch wild beasts with snares, and deceive [birds] with birdlime,
when the hopes of the youths are raised, and [she takes on] fury-driven limbs,
she indeed, with sweet enticements, [works] upon wretched mortals,
so that nothing be left untried -- with the lyre and tuneful strings,
she thoroughly assails the senses, and has caught flame in the tinder,
but the youth, in whose bones a great fire is stirred by
harsh love; for indeed care grants no rest to his limbs,
he cannot stand still in one place. He burns, feverish with sudden hope,
and he lifts up his spirit, and thunders dreadfully with his arms,
and he wearies his swift steed with iron-shod heel,
from whose crest rise swan's feathers,
his cloak embroidered with the needle, and bright with Iberian rust-red,
hurling missiles with his hand, he cleaves the flying breezes,
displaying [his] skill, and fixes his gaze upon the maiden,
and he, frantic in spirit, [puts on] his shield and, triple-woven with gold,
puts on his breastplate, [and] with force seizes a strong spear,
raging through the city, and stirs up mock battles under arms,
it rises to heaven -- the shout of men and the blare of trumpets.
then, having gone off from here, he paces to the rich altars.
And now this way, now that, he traces uncertain circles,
as once, whirling, a top under the twisted lash,
at times [his] knees fail [him], and he refuses the course;
he grows faint, dying; he has besieged the threshold of [his] beloved.
The wretched first-fruits of the youth, and through the shadow of the earth,
shrieking, nor does he close his eyes in sweet sleep.
What was he to do? soothing his sick love with the lyre,
such things he utters with his voice, he gives a groan from the depths of his breast.
O glory of Italy, maiden, my greatest care,
you have no pity on me, you drive me at last to die;
conquered by love of you, having endured winds and rains,

div.note: The [male] member is called 'Priapus' in Italian.

lg.l: at dead of night I came, a suppliant, to [your] threshold.
By you, by the parents who begot you such as you are,
give your right hand to a wretched man; not one night more
this last favor I beg, have pity on [my] toils,
kindly one, I pray, have pity, on a mind bearing what it does not deserve.
Nor am I so ill-favored, O one of the blood of nymphs.
O how often, and what things has Galatea said to us!
Unhappy, she burns; for she wept at my leaving.
Perhaps she also makes vows, while I trace your footsteps,
and Phoebus loves me, if my songs can do anything;
always your honor and name and praises will remain.
Only remain true to [your] promises, beneath the silent night;
make use of your lot, [you who have been] idle through so many years,
by making excuses you draw out our love at length,
nor does my resolve, now shifted from its place, yield.
Whom do you flee, ah madwoman? is this the faith [you] promised?
Stay your step; who keeps you from our embraces?
O you joined to a worthy husband, fortune overturns all things;
nowhere is faith safe; to break off [this] cruel life
my mind remains unmoved; ah, what [earth] might now gape deep enough,
for me — but you, O winds, rather take pity,
and hear our prayers, and of [my] fierce grief
carry some part back, O winds, to the ears of the gods;
arise, some avenger, from my bones!
This I pray, this last utterance I pour forth with [my] blood.
The lovely heifer [i.e. the girl] recognized the groan from afar,
wearing a maiden's face and garb, and with laughter unrestrained,
she makes for the lofty roofs, and from the highest peak of the stable
— for who, most presumptuous of youths, bade you
approach our home? I feared no such thing of you —
cease to inflame both me and yourself with your complaints.
This is the way; where the road leads you, direct your step.
Having said this she falls silent; she mocked the lover with vain hope.
She shut herself within [her] house, where her former husband, to her,
exulting with joy, and turned [toward her] with his horse's sinew,
gave [her] the longed-for embraces, and loosed [her] cares.
Rich in wealth, rich in embroidered robe and gold;
here [is] the hearth, and the fat pine-torches, the strongest wines,
soft chestnuts, and feasts set out before [their] eyes,
with kingly luxury; the flute gives forth its twofold strain,
and renews the dances; he, harsh and reckless in his wrath,
and just as a wolf lying in wait at a full sheepfold
rages against the absent [flock], and terrifies the sky with [clashing] arms;
light with [his] bare sword, and inglorious with [his] blank shield,
then shame and courage conscious [of itself] kindle [his] strength;
he batters at the gates, and the posts made hard with a bar,
the unhappy poet, much taken by empty hope,
groaning much over [his] disgrace, [he turns his] steps back,
retraces them unhurried, inflamed with great love;
he looks back, ignorant of [what has happened], and ungrateful for [his] safety.
Meanwhile it snows just the same through the whole sky;
they, taking turns, with quivering tongues [each other's] mouths
they gather with [their] mouths; joys thrill through [their] silent breast,
embracing each other they linger through night and day.
Alas, pitiable boy, what madness has seized you?
Where are you rushing, doomed to die, [like] a drone to another's fodder?
The glory of such great things deceives you, unwary [as you are];
O beautiful boy, do not trust too much to [your] complexion.
[His] strong hands availed nothing, nor the light of [his] youth,
purple/radiant [though it was]; she cares nothing for the gods, nothing for songs.
and the fate-bringing sword, the breastplate stiff with bronze,
the swift-footed horses draped in purple, and the flowing crests,
it delights [her] to gather plunder, and to live by pillage;
this is [her] love, this [her] zeal — the common Fury of [her] country —
that she may drink from a jeweled [cup], and sleep in Tyrian purple;
she feeds on the entrails of the wretched, and on black blood;
for mad hunger urges [her] on, and she gnaws and drags
the soft flock, mute with fear, according to ancient custom,
[those] bringing gifts — now these, now those, she receives.
In the midst of the halls, opportunity is granted to speak face to face;
then at last, admitted, they revisit the longed-for pools.
But others, kept far off, the shore bars away;
for a hundred years they wander, [their] tears rolling in vain.
Gorgons, Harpies, to be tamed at great cost,
they drive the idle drones, [that worthless] herd, from the hives;
I speak of no unknown things: to the great city of Mars
never did [my] hand come home heavy with bronze;
by this snow-white gift of wool, O Moon, did [he] deceive you,
Pan, guardian of sheep — for the seer knows all things —
calling [you] into the deep groves; nor did you scorn [him] calling.
What will the mistresses do? — girls plying [their] wool-tasks —
and they sought for themselves a memorial and pledge of love,
and a mantle, and a veil embroidered with saffron acanthus.
Having observed these things, and having followed these examples,
O comrades, turn your minds to what I shall say:
vast [store of] silver gives laws to the fathers summoned,
holding the scepter; and he softens [their] spirits, and tempers [their] wrath.
In the midst of the frosts he inflamed [her] heart with love,
and gave hope to [her] wavering mind, and loosed [her] modesty;
he bursts through the threshold, and tears the doorposts from the hinge.
Wherefore come now, o youths, if pleasure so inclines in [your] heart
to burst the bars with [your] hand, and to swim the Stygian marsh
in the shapeless mire — give lilies with full hands

div.note: They call the vulva the 'Stygian swamp'.
The lilies [refer to] French gold coins.

lg.l: Golden — now she was seen as the one salvation for the dying
Before the doors, suddenly creaking on their hinge — the sacred [doors]
The gates are thrown open, and the jaws of heavy-reeking Avernus
But flee, o wretched ones, flee hence — a snake lurks in the grass
breathing [into you] a viperous spirit — the wanton girl
when she will give embraces, and will plant sweet kisses
bare at the knee, her flowing garment gathered with a knot
You take to flight, your legs stripped of their buskins
to touch [it is] unlawful — such a breath from black [jaws]
pouring itself forth from [its] throat, strikes the nostrils with its smell
Here a turbid whirlpool, with its vast abyss, [muddy] with mire
opens its plague-bearing jaws; impious Rage [dwells] within
and pale Diseases dwell beneath the hollowed rock
where the wide approaches lead, a grove looms over with its shade
bristling from above; and beneath every leaf they cling
Foul birds, monsters of every kind of wild beast
too well known to the wretched — you see what sort of guard
O youth outstanding in courage — night and day
sits in the vestibule, and in the first jaws of Orcus
more savage within holds its seat — the harshest realm
Pale Tisiphone, and the Chimaera armed with flames
Here [is] that labor of the house, and the inextricable maze
Alas, flee the cruel lands, flee the greedy shore
Learn virtue from me, boy, and not to scorn the gods
It is right for no chaste person to set foot on the accursed threshold
The huge gate facing [us], dark, breathes out a foul stench
whence the hollow pools sweat with warm moisture
Here [are] those whom harsh Love has consumed with cruel wasting
Overwhelmed by the waves, the swift whirlpool devours them in its flood
snatching the view from their eyes — a huge abyss
Unaware of crimes, and youth in its earliest flower

div.note: He calls the vulva 'Avernus' (the mouth of the underworld).

lg.l: whether driven by wandering of the way, or by storms
they plunge headlong into the shoals; they are rolled in the lowest depth
and in the miry lake, having suffered wounds in fighting
purple with crests, youths gleaming with gold
and feeble old men, to attempt the labor of young men
All dared it — a monstrous crime — and gained possession of what they dared
Why should I pursue greater things? A race unconquerable in war
of great-souled heroes — [the race] cruelly mangled in the face —
his face and both hands — he is whirled along in black gloom
through banks seething with pitch and black whirling abyss
and those who were chaste priests while life remained
and those who [were] pious bards — truly this is that Charybdis
of these crags Helenus, of these dreadful rocks, used to sing
Gods, forbid these threats; gods, avert such a fate
Take this life of mine instead, by whatever death
If I perish, it will be a comfort to have perished by the hands of men
Scattered [men] are seen swimming in the vast flood
saved from the waves — few, whom the just [Jupiter] loved
Jupiter, or [that] wood once venerable to sailors
brought [it] back to a better [state]; than which nothing [is] more immediately [effective]
help comes, and drives the black poisons from [the] limbs
and opens the vast shoals, and calms the sea
The one safety for the conquered — the remedy for our madness
Why should I recount to you [things] sweating from fragrant wood
the faces of men, eaten away by sad disease and filth
to grow green with new foliage, having forgotten their former sap
boil its roots in fragrant wine
(This is done when the Zephyrs first stir the waves
with the sun newly risen) — and it is not long before [a] huge [growth]
and a shaggy eyebrow, and a long beard
sprouts from the root, and unfolds all its leaves

div.note: Made hairless on account of the French disease (syphilis).
Holy wood (guaiac wood), a remedy for the French disease (syphilis).

lg.l: Phillyrides Chiron and Amythaonian Melampus
Often too they shake [them] with running, and tire [them] with sun
youths experienced in war, and the unarmed crowd
and long-lived old men; sweat flows in streams on every side
the flaw is boiled out, and useless moisture sweats away
it removed the congealed stain; labor conquers all
Every region places sure health in this art
Yet not every evil for the wretched, nor utterly all
bodily plagues depart, [leaving] reminders of grief
burning pustules — [these] do not leave [them] even in death itself
I do not wish to embrace all things in my verses
Not such power [is] in [my] mind — long-haired Iopas with his lyre
sounds forth on his golden [lyre] — what unworthy cause, serene [as it was],
marred [his] face, and the last coils of [his] tail
of half-human Cacus, from which founder our race [descends]
with barriers burst, by what force the deep seas swell
Happy is he who could approach the realms of Nature
through places rough with neglect, and escape upward to the air above
having dared moreover [to go] beyond even the Garamantes and the Indians
to attempt unknown paths, and the practice of healing
admiring the venerable gift of the fateful wand
whether on the banks of the Po, or beside the pleasant Adige
He sings; the calm winds have smoothed the waters
and the rivers, changed, have rested from their courses
indeed the very bands, and the echoing rocks, were astonished;
the chorus of the Nereids and of Phorcus, [and] every race of swimming things
they stood fixed with astonished minds — o divine Poet
What gifts, what gifts, shall I give you in return for such a song?
As for what remains, I will pursue [only] the highest points of the matter
I will set forth in words — the vein leaping with blood
blood-red, huge, rising up from the lowest valleys

div.note: Fracastoro, who wrote about the French disease (syphilis).
This is what Italians call the priapus (penis).

lg.l: Although [my] mind shudders to remember, and shrinks back in grief
from the groin of the viperous brood poison drips down
the serpent's maddening evil, [and] the foulest [filth] of the belly
the discharge, which wicked stepmothers have often gathered
For it lays waste to everything far and wide, beneath a vast whirlpool,
it breaks out, and holds everything far and wide covered in mire,
and it corrupted the pools, infected the pastures with corruption,
the backs of swine, and it blights the iron with salty rust,
fearing this, watch the months and stars of heaven —
the Father himself established what the monthly moon might counsel.
Straightway the sick have a different fever; the face — a rough
gauntness disfigures [it]; pallor at once seizes the countenance.
Observe likewise the garments, the familiar coverings,
the foul rites, and the huge bolts of the gates;
a black stench rolls through the halls, and with copious blood
earth and couches are drenched, and barbarous coverings of the legs;
Eridanus, king of rivers, with the rainy Kids [constellation],
with rushing eddies, and golden with much sand,
cannot at all blot out with waters those bloody spoils,
nor fair Ganges, nor Nile with its rich stream,
then indeed, thunderstruck, and torpor grips their listless eyes,
with silent eyes, and by their touch they foul everything
[a touch] unclean; then they seek shelter, then they tend their bodies,
their foul limbs with filth — the breathing-vents of savage Dis.
And all, sluggish with hunger, linger within the halls,
but not sluggish in love and nighttime wars —
although at that time the lioness, forgetful of her cubs,
wandered more savage over the plains; then the fiercest tigress,
yet none [of them] ever followed such base [couplings] of beasts
as this mating — what such great madness has seized [your] mind,
O nymphs of Europe and Asia, surpassing in form?
Has such confidence in your lineage possessed you?
O the crime! Behold, even the monuments of unspeakable lust,
Pasiphae, and the mingled breed, and the two-formed offspring [Minotaur]!
But hope that the gods are mindful of right and wrong.
And the herds return to mating on fixed days,
an iron breed, with which none could vie
either to flow so abundantly, or to endure for as many years.
into frenzy and fire they rush, beneath the sign of Cancer,
and when gloomy winter [comes], or when rainy spring rushes in,
and when to their first matings the pleasure, now well-known,
arouses them, [when] only the scent has brought familiar breezes,
they have abandoned their homes, and demand generative seed,
night and day, and following the clashing bronze,
it delights [them] to drive flying chariots to the shrines,
often a day and a night, and a whole month in order,
under the burning sun, and under the axis of the cold heaven,
over rocks and crags, it delights [them] to indulge in dances,
and they put on dreadful faces of hollowed bark,
and now neither the bridles of men, nor cruel lashes,
with the hide of a whole ox, nor do obstacles hold them back —
the rivers, nor can wretched parents call them back;
nay even, shut in darkness and blind prison,
(may it be right for me to tell what I have heard) and unwed maidens
then, trembling, they come together among themselves, and often without any
unions, made pregnant by the wind — wondrous to tell —
before her years; and the maiden dares to clash with men,
dreadful to tell — am I to trust in this monster?
With this monster once vented horrible wrath
the instigator of crimes, at the first origin of the growing world,
thrust down lofty souls to the Stygian waves.
Thence the race of men and cattle, and the painted birds,
to rush toward the worse, and slide back, carried backward,
alas, piety! alas, the ancient faith of ancestral valor!
Almighty Father, who ratifies covenants with his thunderbolt,
then first he added evil venom to black serpents,
and everywhere checked the wine that ran in streams,
and shook the honey from the leaves; mortal hearts
the long-awaited crop mocked [them] with empty oats.
Justice, departing from the earth — pitiful to behold —
fled first; there come diseases, and sad old age,
and Fear, and Hunger the ill-counselor, and shameful Want,
and the madness of war, and the love of possession took its place.
or the frenzied forum; then Earth, in unnatural birth,
creates Coeus and Iapetus, and the proud brothers.
From that time, sent forth into the light from Stygian darkness,
vain Superstition, which, scattered through the great world,
then the Father scattered with his thunderbolt the heaped-up mountains,
and the brothers conspiring to breach heaven,
and scattered the ships, and overturned the seas with winds.
Hence flocks, herds, men, every race of wild beasts,
and whatever monsters the sea bears beneath its marbled surface —
mingling in a flood, he hurls [them] onto hidden rocks,
and dashes them on the shoals, and girds them with a mound of sand.
The heavens thundered, clouds girded the sky,
and impious generations feared eternal night.
From that flood, we all pay the penalties,
for the offense and madness of one — a maiden doomed to die,
the cause of so great an evil, terrified by the warnings of the gods,
not unpunished indeed, having experienced the pains of Lucina,
now too she fills the region far and wide with sad laments —
alas, the hated brood — the maiden who marveled at the [golden] apples —
it is right for men to hate her brood and all her future race,

div.note: You shall give birth in pain (Gen. 3:16).

lg.l: yet we press on, forgetful, and blind with frenzy,
we join hands in hospitality, and enter beneath the roof.
united souls — thus, thus it delights [us] to go beneath the shades,
O fatherland, O [Mantua], too near, alas, to wretched Cremona,
Mantua, rich in forebears — cast this care from your breast;
let them celebrate such marriages, and such wedding-hymns,
Brontes, and Steropes, and Pyracmon, naked of limb,
a race of men born of tree-trunks and hard oak,
nor to be turned [into] the impious horns of the long-lived stag,
and the hideous forehead — what first dangers shall I avoid?
O too fortunate, [they who] have hated the whole race,
of women — as for me, no day, in such bold daring,
so shall it prove [me] unlike, so long as breath shall rule these limbs.
Learn, blessed souls, and you, best of seers,
Would it not have been better to turn aside the goads of Love,
with constant hunting, and to try remote lands,
through various chances, through so many crises of affairs,
and through waves, with the sea surging, and through pathless rocks,
than once to have seen the shapeless [monster] beneath the vast cave,
Scylla, girt about the loins with barking monsters,
and the grove, dark with black dread.
But the fierce mind of Cacus, [maddened] by furies, and dire desire
goad and urge [it] to provoke unknown wars.
What does it profit to indulge so greatly in mad toil,
What new madness is this? What madness has driven you,
alas, wretched citizens, to throw [your] arms about [their] neck
in a wretched embrace, with heavily-breathing serpents?
Do not, boys, do not accustom your minds to such great wars,
nor arm your hands — [ye] dire and obscene birds,
they turn mighty spirits about in a narrow breast,
more in spring, because in spring warmth returns to the bones; they

div.note: Italians call a man whose wife is unfaithful 'horned' (a cuckold).
This is what Italians call the priapus (penis).

lg.l: Then indeed, burning, they join battle with great force,
nor could we strive against, nor hold out so far,
[our] strength does not suffice, with feet linked in mutual coils,
I sing no uncertain things: we stood against the cruel weapons,
and joined battle, with neither the gods nor strength equal:
Then first youth was clothing my cheeks with down,
and strong in limbs and bulk, [yet] confused, unarmed,
after [my] beard, growing whiter, fell beneath the shears,
I snatched myself, I confess, from death, and broke the chains,
of the Acidalian mother; arms laid aside, inglorious,
No safety [is] in war, O youths, bravest hearts,
lay aside [your] hopes; take care lest arms clash with arms.
Their anger is beyond measure; who [could tell] in song the slaughters
so various, and the death of leaders, who in speaking the funerals
could unfold, or could grasp all the forms of crimes,
How great [a storm], through the Idaean [plains], poured forth from savage Mycenae,
went over the fields — [all] confess that they know [it],
