and the Morini, farthest of men — a woman [was] leader of the deed,
shakes the foundations, and lays Troy low from its roof-top,
smoking with a pitch-black whirlwind, and with glowing ash,
he himself, the Mycenaean, leader of the great Achivi,
victor by swift Simois beneath lofty Ilium,
by the hand of [his] wicked wife, at the very threshold,
he fell, and poured out [his] life with much blood.
With spells Circe changed the companions of Ulysses;
Juno's heavy wrath, and [her] insatiable heart—
a man remarkable for piety — by land and by sea
whirls, driving [him] round — the faith promised to Sychaeus's ashes,
not kept. Could Pallas burn the fleet
of the Argives, and sink the men themselves in the sea?
Why should I recall the fleets burned on the Erycinian shore,
Why should I recall Alcides, destroyed by an unworthy death?
and hearts that know not how to be softened by human prayers,
they scattered the young man, torn apart, over the wide fields,
[him] who was soothing tigers, and driving oaks along with [his] song;
I shudder to tell it — in one single marriage-night,
the band of youths foully slain, and the bloody bridal-chambers,
Alas, does so great a crime fall upon anyone? — by a stepmother's cunning,
a boy, marking his unshorn cheeks with first youth,
thrown from the chariot, dying, he rolls upon the fields,
torn apart by the maddened horses. Who, in telling such things,
could refrain from tears? Notorious through the whole world,
and Scylla pays the penalty for the purple lock,
Shall I speak, or be silent? — for a mother, with her children's blood,
to stain her hands? O ruler of highest Olympus,
O father, must it be thought that any [souls] go hence to heaven?
Do you see these things? Or, father, when you hurl [your] thunderbolts,
do we shudder in vain? [Is there any region] not full of our suffering,
what region on earth? With no distinction, savage slaughter
she stirs up, and lets loose all the reins of [her] wrath,
raging like a torrent of water, or a black whirlwind,
the savage force of [her] spirit drives lovers to contend with one another,
with frequent wounds, [and drives them] to betray their masters' hands
unhappy monster, than which none [is] more outstanding,
vomiting fires from [its] mouth — [she] can arm brothers, of one mind, for battles,
and overturn homes with hatreds; she lays all things low far and wide,
Woman — the nations wandering scattered from either shore,
she terrifies, as [she terrifies] feeble birds, and fierce peoples,
she tracks, searching, and disembowels with hooked talons,
[those] forgetful of [their] kingdoms, and caught by base desire,
having ventured a greater crime, and begun a greater madness,
within [her] native walls, splendid with royal luxury,
amid the sacred rites of the gods, [and] youths before the faces of [their] parents,
she lays low through various mischances — with womanly weapons
she sends down to death many bodies of men in her path,
rolling [her] bloody gaze, she roars with bloody mouth,
she sows various rumors — she for whom sad wars
and wraths, and treacheries, and harmful crimes are dear to [her] heart,
O son of the highest father, to pay worthy thanks
it is not within our power to have escaped [this] wicked race;
for what remains, I pray, make firm your divine will more closely [upon us],
she turns over in her heart tricks and dire wickedness,
Snatch me, unconquered one, from these evils — the first way of safety [is this]:
to you I flee for refuge; we all beg you for peace,
together, all the foremost of the youth, and the ancient Quirites,
look upon us — a war must be waged with a dread race,
no grimmer monster than they — a cold horror [comes over] me,
it shakes my limbs, and I tremble at the sound of feet and voice,
for she saps [my] strength little by little, and burns [me] by the sight [of her],
WOMAN — gods, avert such a plague from the earth!
Nymphs, our love, let us sing of things a little greater.
Amid the arms of kings, with a great tumult raging,
The shepherd Aristeus, adorned with leaves of the olive,
[Son] of fatidic Manto, and son of the Tuscan river,
With ancestral songs, at the wave of the Tiberine river,
Looking up at the sky, with tears thus welling forth, he speaks:
Alas, why have such great clouds girded the sky?
The heavens have thundered, and the winds, as if drawn up in column,
changed [in course], roar aslant; through the sky there goes, turbid, [a storm of weapons],
a storm of weapons, and an iron rain rushes on.
Burning shields, and gleaming bronze, I see.
The din of arms, through all the sky, Germania
heard, and horns resounded with a hoarse blare;
and trembling mothers pressed their children to their breasts.
The causes of war stand fixed. Behold, again the cruel fates, backward—
call [us] back; impious Mars rages through the whole world.
A youth outstanding in beauty, seeking a new kingdom,
a dark day carried off, and plunged in bitter death.
Alas, pitiable boy, [of] race from the lofty blood of the gods,
Fortune begrudged you, that you might not see the kingdom,

div.note: The Duke of Orléans, son of King Francis of France.

lg.l: nor the fields of Ausonia, ever retreating backward,
By your death the Alps trembled with unaccustomed tremors;
the waves shook, and the earth, terrified to its depths,
of Italy — and every plowman fled the fields,
and every farmer, and [all] driven to a different shore,
the shepherds of sheep: the deep woods resounded
with the bleating of flocks, and the rivers with frequent lowing;
for you the clear lakes wept; near to Cremona,
and the earth too is sprinkled with tears, and the Dryad maidens,
beside the water, where the great [river] wanders with slow windings —
the Eridanus, king of rivers, pitiable to see —
built countless pyres. For you, LILIES [fleurs-de-lis], in full
behold, the nymphs bring in baskets, solaces for grief,
small, for [a grief] so vast, yet owed to a wretched father;
you [were] all the glory of your own. After the fates took you away,
discord arose among the kings with great commotion;
hence Augustus Caesar, driving the Italians into battle,
who demands for himself the kingdom of Italy, and the first honors,
wields thunderbolts; his proud emblem of war [is]
the fierce [bird], glaring grimly, Jove's armor-bearer, with hooked talons —
around him countless peoples; and the peoples of Latium,
and Hesperia, great and rich in the metals of the Chalybes,
and the Morini, farthest of men, and the two-horned Rhine,
and the turbid Ister, rolling its yellow sands —
but on the other side [he] snatches up a strong spear by force,
a king of outstanding lineage: he demands that honor be restored to him,
of fertile Ausonia, and the dowry sought with blood;
and he calls the gods to witness that he is again being forced to battle,
rising up on high, and brandishing the great LILIES [fleurs-de-lis],
he calls the ranks to arms. One day against the Roman citadels
[he will bring] great destruction, and will let loose the open Alps.

div.note: The lilies, emblem of the King of France.
The lilies, emblem of the King of France.

lg.l: each man for himself strains with the utmost force of his might;
they who now [hoped] for themselves rest from battle, and safety for their affairs,
were hoping — now they want arms, and weary Mars,
armed with iron, and gleaming, heads held high with crests.
Where are you rushing? And what is this sudden discord that arises?
What is this strange new madness? What fortune, [you who were] at peace,
disturbs [you]? Is there such great wrath in heavenly minds?
No, boys, do not accustom your minds to such great wars,
both alike in spirit, both distinguished by outstanding arms —
nor turn your strong might into the vitals of your fatherland.
O restrain your wrath: let right hands join in treaties
where it is granted; but beware lest arms clash with arms.
And you, first, spare [them], bravest LEADER of the Italians,
nor let so dire a desire of ruling come upon you;
known to you already is what he has suffered, by land and by sea.
There is no safety in war: we all beg peace of you,
mothers and men, and boys bereft of their parents,
curse this dire war. Shield the Latins with peace —
already worn out by every misfortune, destitute of everything.
Why should I recount the unspeakable slaughters, and the deserted realms
of the shepherds, and the pastures empty far and wide?
Still with our blood the Tiberine streams grow warm;
for Latium I entreat, for the majesty of your kin —
cast the weapons from your hand. Let both [peoples], under equal laws,
unconquered nations, enter into an everlasting treaty.
Now I return to you, great father, and to your counsels;
to you I flee for refuge, and, a suppliant, [to you,] best King of kings —
why do you try the city big with wars, and hearts made harsh,
to the Ausonian shore [?] — what very great valor could
have been, it was; the whole body of the Realm contended.
Cease now at last, and be bent by our prayers,

div.note: He calls him Francis, King of France.

lg.l: yield to god, and let no man's violence overcome you,
rather, [give] your daughter to an outstanding son-in-law — and this one thing, before all others,
I shall proclaim, and repeating it again and again I shall urge —
grant [this], father, and join this peace with an everlasting treaty.
To what end the sword, or why these weapons, useless in the hands of this people?
But if such great love is in your mind, if such great desire,
to press foreign fields under the yoke, and carry off plunder,
prepare your arms in spirit — for indeed the enemy is not far
for you to seek. The fight is joined on the very threshold
of Ausonia — what such great cowardice has come into your minds?
Behold the fierce enemy, distinguished by the slaughtered Achaeans,
victor from the peoples of the Dawn: and he threatens the highest [citadels],
[threatening] to cast down the citadels of the Italians, and give [them] to ruin —
I shudder in relating it — and let the Latins sit and watch:
the ruler of Asia, laden with the spoils of the East,
like a monstrous tiger among sluggish cattle —
to seek scattered places of exile, and sundry lands
we shall be forced, we who now sit idle on our fields.
They rush with arms into the kingdoms. Cruel everywhere
the grief, everywhere the dread; they bend their bows with strength,
they spur on their horses; at once, from every side, they pour forth weapons,
thick as snow, girded with shining arms,
straining, they charge with spears; the greater part [hurl] leaden
bullets, livid, scattering [them]: the ground smokes with sulphur,
with hollow bronze, and suddenly the whole sky thunders with a crash,
and no long interval passes, when a clamor to the ears
of warring young men, and of those falling beneath harsh Mars —
meanwhile the city walls are thrown into confusion with varied grief;
and now the priests, to the great city of Mars,
clothed in linen, hasten, and encircle it with dances,
the halls; lamps hang from the gilded ceiling-panels.

div.note: He calls 'hollow bronze' what in Italian is called an arquebus.

lg.l: and they implore the gods, around the kindled altars;
without delay, weeping, they hasten, and, adorned with purple,
the sorrowful fathers weep and murmur, and the poor SENATE —
the helmsman himself, to whom belongs the highest power over affairs,
while, most just, he alone offers himself as mediator for peace,
seeing all things, is tossed on the great tide of cares;
he entreats the peace of the gods, and loosens the fillets
of his consecrated head, stretching his palms to the stars,
lest anything be left untried — conspicuous in Tyrian purple,
a boy, marking his unshorn cheeks with the first [down of] youth,
bearing his grandfather's name, to the august walls of the King,
goes and returns along the way so many times, weeping and groaning,
and holds out in his hand a branch of peace-bearing olive,
bearing, beyond his years, a mind and a manly care.
He himself, sitting, guides the rudder, and tends the sails,
now older, but his old age tough as a god's, and green with strength.
Therefore a great council, and the foremost of his own,
summoned by [his] command, now beside pleasant Athesis [the Adige],
he orders to go — [those] whose judgment in mind is better —
shall give laws, and statutes to the men, and the rites of the sacred things.
O father, O eternal power over men and gods,
I hope indeed, if ancient piety at all [regards] the toils
[if it] regards human [affairs], that the crime and the head of these evils
will drain punishments, torn in his whole body,
and in the Roman forum to be burned with crackling flame —
it will be given to see. Do you dare to raise such vast turmoil,
an unbridled race of men, subject to the seven [stars] of the north?
Has such great confidence in your lineage possessed you?
But hope that the gods are mindful of right and wrong.
You yourselves shall pay these penalties with sacrilegious blood.
Learn justice, being warned, and not to scorn the gods.

div.note: Alludes to Augsburg, city of Germany.

lg.l: Son of the highest father, and you, O most holy prophetess,
who guard the Tuscan Tiber, and the Roman palaces —
divine mother, be present, and succor our labor;
and your Romans, tossed upon the whole sea,
gods of the sea and of the land, and powerful over the storms,
amid these disturbances, with such great waves rising,
grant an easy path to the wind, and blow favorably,
and, being calm, preserve the pious, and the toga-clad race —
let there be Latium, let there be Alban kings through the ages,
let their chaste descendants abide in this observance,
and children's children, and those who shall be born from them.
But you, great father, and the priest in pure vesture,
and you, O father Tiber, with your holy stream —
endure, and preserve yourselves for kinder circumstances.
O you who have suffered heavier things, God will give an end to these too.
As long as rivers run to the sea — spread through the world —
inviolate faith shall inhabit the immovable rock of the Capitol,
shall dwell beside [it], and the Roman father shall hold empire,
sent into command, to whom the stars of heaven are obedient,
and the infernal lakes, and the walls of lofty Rome.
He sings: the calm winds have smoothed the seas,
it thundered on the left [in a good omen], and a flash quivering from the sky
puts to flight the gathered clouds, and brings back the sun.
The sun having newly risen, near the great city of Mars,
Leaning upon a smooth olive-staff, DAMON thus began:
Undertake, O, great honors — the time will soon be at hand —
dear offspring of the gods, second hope of great Rome,
all hail to you for your fresh valor, boy, divine poet:
What are you devising? Or with what hope do you now wander in the mountains,
relying on the Thracian lyre and tuneful strings?
Cease now at last, conspicuous in Tyrian purple,
and to dwell in lowly cottages, and to shoot deer;
enjoy your [own] lot; let the Latonian guardian of the groves
herself inhabit the grassy river-banks, and the sunken valleys,
and bring yourself hither, since the fates now demand you —
a greater god drives [you], and sends [you] back to greater works,
[you] who soothe tigers, and move oaks with your song.
it is better to still the waves of Europe and of Asia;
this is virtue's task: do not, brother, forsake your brother.
He indeed, adorned with the leaves of the trimmed olive,
gives laws throughout the peoples, and aims his path toward Olympus.
bearing, beyond his years, a spirit and a manly care,
and you, be present, and run through, together, the labor begun;
take this man as a companion in counsel, and join him to yourself, willing;
both alike in spirit, both distinguished in piety or in arms,
take counsel for the common good, and succor weary affairs.
Come hither, O beautiful boy: for you, lilies in full [baskets] —
behold, the Nymphs bring in their baskets — [those lilies,] your father's emblem;
then the other chieftains, joyful, [bring] whatever store belongs to each —
they bring gifts, and load the altars, and sacrifice young bulls.
Come hither, and even now grow accustomed to being invoked with vows;
many a victim shall fall before your altars by our right hand.
While I myself am mindful of myself, while breath shall rule these limbs,
always shall you be honored by my worship, always celebrated with gifts;
the whole grove shall sing of you, if my songs can do anything at all.
Then all your race — a race from the lofty blood of the gods —
O ancestral gods, under whose divine will Rome ever stands,
do not forbid this youth at least to bring succor to a ruined age;
enough now, with so many years already slipping by,
have we paid all the penalties and punishments of our crimes.
The horn-bearing river, ruler of the Hesperian (western) waters —
this is the man, this is he, whom you so often hear promised to you:
at his coming, the immovable rock of the Capitol,
rearing itself aloft, shall hide its head among the clouds.
Hoary Faith, and Vesta, Quirinus with his brother Remus,
shall give laws: amid the clamor of men, and the zeal of those who favor [him],
behold how all things rejoice at the age that is to come!
they themselves cast up their voices to the stars in joy —
the unshorn mountains [themselves]: the chorus of birds in the fields,
and the joyful flocks, and the ravens exulting in their throats.

div.note: The lilies, emblem of the House of Farnese.

lg.l: Behold, the breezes of the windy murmur have died down.
The sea's surface is laid smooth by its waters; the clouds flee from the vast sky;
The bounteous field teems with birth, and with Zephyr's warm breezes
the fields loosen their folds; subject to no one's care,
the most just earth pours forth easy sustenance from the ground.
therefore delight [seizes] the eager woods, and the rest of the countryside,
and it holds Pan, and the shepherds, and the sister Nymphs,
and the great-hearted leaders, and the walls of lofty Rome:
part exercise their limbs on the grassy wrestling-grounds,
part beat out dances with their feet, and sing songs;
and, joyful, they arrange mutual feasts among themselves,
and they put on fearsome faces of hollowed bark.
The whole grove resounds with the din, and with unrestrained laughter
cease the Maenalian verses, now cease, o flute,
we shall sing songs better then, when he himself shall have come.
O glory of Italy, once, while life remained,
holding the scepter, where mighty [it] wanders with slow windings,
[the] Mincius, and fringes its banks with tender reed,
always shall you be honored with worship of mine, always celebrated with gifts,
While I am mindful of myself, while breath shall rule these limbs,
Hail, true offspring of Jove. You are that greatest one,
the only one who [aids] us, while a great tumult throws [all] into confusion,
bearing, beyond his years, a spirit and a manly care,
you raise up spirits of your own accord with your words, and with steadfast heart
towering, holding your weapons, [and] troops gleaming with bronze,
raging in the manner of a torrent of water, and the rebellious Gaul
you lay low upon the ground, and the vast plains grow white with bones,
Parthenope [Naples], never unmindful of so great a service,
your right hand is the cause; she has taken her seat upon the ancestral throne.
Why should I recount those spoils hanging from your rooftops,
already made known [to all]? With what praises should I liken you to heaven,
flower of the ancients, and valor of men? Whose is the care [to tend] the gleaming
horses at pasture, that they may await the rewards of their well-earned palm,
in Europe and Asia — so great is the care for victory.
You [are] every glory to your own people, you most observant of justice,
exhausted now by the misfortunes of all, needy of everything,
you unite [them] with city and home. Your fame, spread throughout the lands,
gifts besides, of gold and solid ivory,
they have joined to you (all confess that they know it),
the ruler of Asia, a race unconquerable in war,
and the Britons, sundered utterly from the whole world,
Hail, holy father, bravest leader of the Italians,
blessed in your offspring of men, if my songs can avail anything,
always shall your honor, and your name, and your praises remain.

div.note: The army of Charles VIII, King of France.
Henry, King of Britain (England); father of Hercules and Ferdinand.

lg.l: O youth outstanding in spirit, to whom the royal power submits,
Rich in wealth, rich in embroidered raiment, and in gold,
A city Etruscan in soil, and most fierce in pursuits of war,
Flower of the ancients, and valor of men, after many [deaths] of your kin,
deaths, after the varied labors of men and of the city,
you have come at last, a god sent from high heaven.
I believe indeed — nor is the faith an empty one — that [your] lineage is of the gods,
a boy, marking his unshorn cheeks with first youth,
within his native walls, amid a great disturbing tumult,
sent into great command by the winds of popular favor,
you hold the scepter, for the great King of Olympus willed you [so],
amid these commotions, to bear off an honor set apart,
and by justice granted [you] to still the surging waves of the people(s),
Behold, the breezes of windy murmuring have fallen still;
the safe seas are silent, O bravest leader of the Italians,
go on now, and flying over the sea, spread your sails to the open deep,
with [your] goddess mother showing the way; but the deeds of [your] father —
it would be more profitable to remember — [him] shaggy with bristles,
on his chest. No one could have withstood him with impunity,

div.note: For it was above all his mother who brought it about that her son Cosimo should rule.

lg.l: meeting the armed foe (all confess that they know it),
whether he spurred the flanks of his foaming steed
towering, bearing arms; or when on foot he went against the enemy,
fierce, uttering harsh sounds, rolling flaming eyes.
Moreover, the images of the ancients, the lofty honors of [his] forefathers,
his character, and pursuits, and arms upon the sacred doorposts,
things to be admired by you, and wars fought one after another,
many deeds by a healing [Medici] hand, spread through the whole world,
Son of a goddess — for that you go over the deep under greater
auspices, the assurance is manifest: upon you the faces of the Latins,
turn their eyes; it is right to seek foreign realms,
a greater god is at work, and sends [you] on to greater deeds.
Therefore with all zeal, inflamed by love of praise,
and having followed great-souled leaders and these examples,
dare, and confidently bear your breast against the enemy.
nor let it repent you to endure harsh toils,
under the burning sun, and under the cold axis of the sky,
amid weapons, and to brave threatening rivers,
nights and days; thus did brave Etruria grow.
these shall be your arts, to raise up the mass of walls,
to the Ausonian shore, to launch armed fleets,
to protect Italy, to drive the enemy from [its] borders,
and to gather a band for war, by land and by sea,
to spare the subjected, and to war down the proud.
above all, worship the gods; thus, in the end, as victor
you shall brandish a monstrous weapon in your hand, and fierce peoples
you shall crush, second to none of the ancients in valor,
then all your lineage, [reaching] beyond even the Garamantes and the Indians,
shall extend its dominion, and shall hold sway over all shores,
and the sons of sons, and those who shall be born from them.
these are the things of which it may be granted that you be advised by our voice.

div.note: A citadel at Ilva (Elba), built by him (fragment; initial word truncated).

lg.l: Go, go, our glory; enjoy better fates,
Recalling your grandfather in name, and your father in spirit and hands,
When the shepherd had spoken these words in divine song,
Son of fatidic Manto, and offspring of the Tuscan river,
The father of gods and king of men thundered auspiciously on the left,
He gave his nod, and with that nod shook the whole of Olympus.
Guardian of the beautiful flock, and priest of the gods,
O glory of Italy, iron [hardy] progeny,
Awaited one, in Laurentine soil and in Latin fields,
You have come at last to the Ausonian shore,
So indeed I imagined in my mind, and thought it would come to pass,
Counting the hours, night and day.
They themselves, in joy, toss their voices to the stars,
The unshorn [wooded] mountains of fertile Ausonia,
And the joyful flocks, and ravens exulting in their throats,
With the bleating of flocks the whole grove resounds.
And now every field, now every tree, is bringing forth [its increase],
Now everything smiles, and the safe seas lie silent.
Behold, the nymphs bring you lilies in full baskets,
pale violets, and Cecropian [Attic] thyme,

div.note: This makes plausible the personification of Virgil addressing Cosimo, Duke of Florence, since Virgil is figured as the son of the Tuscan river, for Ocnus, founder of Mantua, traced his origin from it.
The lilies, emblem of the Este family.

lg.l: I myself will gather quinces pale with tender down,
and the hard pear, and chestnuts,
always with honor from me, always shall you be celebrated with gifts,
However things may turn out, while I myself am mindful of myself,
As yearly vows are paid to Bacchus and Ceres, so to you,
In the soft meadows the farmers will make [their offerings];
Behold who gather at the wave of the Tiberine river,
Shepherds of sheep, from the rich stalls.
At your coming, far off the rooftops of the farmhouses are smoking,
And the untamed [hardy] farmers set out their feasts.
In Teutonic fashion they drain the bronze mixing-bowls,
They contend in sport, and roar with joy,
They chant the sacred rites, beat out the dances, the mothers in long procession,
Mothers and men, with songs of their fathers,
Hail, great parent, to the great city of Mars,
Awaited one, you come, seeking familiar shores,
As the vine is a glory to the trees, as grapes are to the vine,
In great Hesperia [Italy], you are the whole glory of your people,
Stay your step, and do not withdraw yourself from our sight.
On our mountains one ought to pasture the sheep.
Here [are] cool springs, and meadows fresh with streams,
Here [is] perpetual spring, twice-breeding flocks,
Add so many outstanding cities, and the toga-clad race,
The great deities of the place, and great-hearted leaders.
Cease now at last to try [reach] distant, hidden lands,
Through rocks and cliffs — here is your sure home,
O best of the Greek-born race, to whom [the god grants] a great mind and spirit,
the Delian seer [Apollo] inspires, O divine poet,
At last you have come to the great city of Mavors [Mars],
through what lands, and over what great seas, [you] borne,
I receive [you], O deservedly the greatest part of our fame,
Son of a goddess, henceforth now forget the lost Greeks:
You shall be ours; hither you bring yourself, with the fates demanding [it],
Here is your certain home; certain — do not depart — [are your] household gods,
Beneath the lofty mountain, which now bears the surname IULUS,
Here [are] cool springs, and meadows fresh with streams,
Here [is] unbroken spring, and summer in months not its own,
Fruits lie strewn everywhere, each beneath its own tree,
Now all things smile, and, plump in the lush grass, [the kids]
the kids struggle among themselves with butting horns,
At your coming, the chariots, poured forth from the barrier, rush on,
In the soft meadows, at the wave of the river Tiber,
youths purple-crested, and gleaming with gold,
they vie in sport, and wrestle on the tawny sand,
the whole grove resounds with the din, and with the eagerness of those cheering,

div.note: It signifies the P[ontifex] M[aximus] (Supreme Pontiff).
This is what certain fields on the bank of the Tiber are called.

lg.l: They themselves, in joy, hurl their voices to the stars,
the unshorn mountains — the rivers have stayed their courses,
From every side, with desire of seeing, the Roman offspring,
pours round about and rushes — boys, and unwed girls,
sing sacred songs, clap out dances, and recite verses,
Hail, holy father, than whom no other is more outstanding,
to draw ash-trees down from the mountains with ancestral songs,
to halt the water in the rivers, and to kindle Mars [war] with song,
Hail, true offspring of Jove, you are that greatest one,
you alone, who for us, now that so many years have slipped away,
show [us] both the sacred springs and the rivers [once] discovered,
therefore delight [seizes] the eager woods, and the rest of the countryside,
holds Pan, and the shepherds; for you, lilies in brimming
behold, the nymphs bring [them] in baskets. You — [whom] mightiest Rome of all the world
Rome worships, and veils [your] temples with green laurel,
and in [her] hand holds forth a branch of peace-bearing OLIVE,
IULIUS, a name descended from great Iulus,
This is the man, this is he, whom you so often hear promised to you,
the flower of the ancients, and the valor of men. He alone the most just,
gives laws to the peoples, and aims his way toward Olympus,
he himself, sitting, holds the helm and tends the sails,
sent into empire, to whom the stars of heaven are obedient,
and the lakes of the underworld, and the walls of lofty Rome,
here, borne by four horses, conspicuous in purple,
victor from the peoples of the Dawn, to the wave of the Tiber,
he shall consecrate an immortal vow to the king of the heaven-dwellers;
unless in vain [my] foolish forefathers taught [me] augury.
A greater work, a greater order of things is born for me,
Fortunate old man, with lyre and tuneful strings,
And you, be present, and run through together the task begun.

div.note: A relative of Julius III, Supreme Pontiff.
The olive is the emblem of Julius III, Supreme Pontiff.

lg.l: Rome, most beautiful, her golden hair torn,
Dear to me above all others.
She stood raging bitterly, at the wave of the river Tiber,
Fearing all things, even things safe.
More sorrowful, and her shining eyes suffused with tears,
Such words she gave.
O glory of Italy, to whom now [belongs] the surname IULUS,
A king, of noble stock.
To thee I flee for refuge, [thee] powerful over heaven and Erebus,
Worshipping suppliantly.
Give your right hand to the wretched woman, with waves rising so high:
The skies thundered.
Together the East Wind and the South Wind rush, as if in marshalled column,
They fell upon the sea.
And gather a foul tempest with black rains,
With waves and with roaring,
Your Romans, a blast hissing with the North Wind,
Bore [them] into hidden shoals.
It strikes the sail head-on. Preserved through many years
Through rocks, and through crags,

div.note: From the north all evil is unleashed (proverbial/biblical tag, cf. Jer. 1:14; here alluding to the Germans/Lutherans).

lg.l: By the reverence of the fathers, the bronze stern trembles under the blows,
And ashen timbers,
And all things threaten the men with instant death.
Up now, break off delay.
Break off delay; be present, and succor our labor,
Again I am borne into arms,
I see blazing shields and gleaming bronze!
On the Trinacrian shore.
A storm of weapons, and an iron rain rushes on,
Behold, the fierce, dreadful enemy,
Victor from the peoples of the Dawn, by land and by sea,
He advances, raging,
Towering, holding his weapons, he races down over the open sea,
Seeking the known shores.
A sound arises on the foaming brine; it echoes round with arms,
Italy! Italy!
To go again into tears, and to leave sweet lands,
Behold, again [it] goads [him] on,
Pursuing with the sword, every ploughman flees across the fields,
And every farmer,
And the earth is bestrewn with tears; everywhere cruel [grief],
grief, everywhere fear.
On this side Euphrates stirs war, on that side Germany,
A race hostile to me,
An unbridled race of men, now with so many years gone by,
(Shall I speak? Or shall I be silent?)
They seized the sacred image, with bloody hands,
They tore apart the hearths,
All dared a monstrous crime, and achieved what they dared,
In the midst of the halls.

div.note: Alludes to the little boat of St. Peter (the Church).
Rome sacked by the Germans in the year 1527.

lg.l: Hence for me came the first taint of evil — ignorant of the gods, [vain superstition]
Vain superstition,
Why should I recount the unspeakable slaughters? Why the monstrous shapes of wild beasts,
Too well known to the wretched?
Still with our blood the streams of the Tiber grow warm,
The earth is soaked with blood.
For Latium I entreat, for the majesty of thy people:
Dear offspring of the gods,
Snatch me, unconquered one, from these evils; one [disaster] is enough and more —
We have seen ruin,
It is thy care to guard the images and temples of the gods,
Within the walls of the fatherland,
To protect Italy, to drive the enemy from her borders,
By the aid of Pallas.
Behold what [forces] gather against me and for the destruction of my own,
Untamed farmers,
The Morini, farthest of men, and the two-horned Rhine,
Calls the columns [of war] to arms,
Shall an impious soldier possess these fields, so well tilled,
A barbarian, these crops?
Discord has brought the wretched citizens — behold, to what [pass]! —
Of fertile Ausonia,
It is driven through the midst of the cities, and the Latin peoples,
Pale Tisiphone.
And she rises up, lifting her torch, and thunders with her mouth,
Powerful through sedition,
But thou, great father, adorned with the leaves of the olive,
Use thy own lot.
Amid the arms of kings, let right hands join in treaties,
To the Ausonian shore.

div.note: The olive and the mount, emblem of the family of Julius III, Supreme Pontiff.

lg.l: There is no safety in war; we all beg thee for peace,
We, thy offspring,
Mothers and men, boys, and unwed maidens,
Hallowed by religion,
They stood transfixed, thunderstruck in mind; toward thee the Latins [turn] their faces,
Turn their eyes.
Come then, dear father, look more closely upon our affairs,
Spare a pious race,
Thus she speaks weeping, and with womanly wailing,
She fell lifeless.
But he [replied]: what such great cowardice has come upon your hearts,
O my offspring?
Spare your fear; the calm winds have smoothed the waters,
Beneath the airy mountain,
Nay, I even build the walls of my longed-for city,
Conquered by love of thee,
Nor be terrified by threats of war; cease to be troubled,
You see all things safe.
Amid these disturbances (this [happens] not without the will of the gods),
Great things await thee too,
Through various chances, through so many crises of affairs,
Unblemished Faith.
Joyful in her brood of gods — beyond both the Garamantes and the Indians,
she shall extend the empire.
Do not doubt; through the midst of the battle-lines, and through the midst of the fires,
The fates will find a way.

div.note: You see 'all is safe' on the coinage of Julius III, Supreme Pontiff.

lg.l: Almighty Fortune, a great and memorable divinity
of Europe and of Asia — for they tell that you give laws,
direct hither the step that wanders over every land,
fiery, through the empty air on swift soles,
or poised over mid-sea upon the swelling wave;
only be present, O, and glide into our hearts.
Kindly one, I pray — struck by a great love of glory,
night and day a suppliant, I invoke your names —
grant an easy course, grant me to extend fame by my deeds,
with my fathers' songs, beyond the Garamantes and the Indians,
close to the edge of Ocean and the setting sun.
Without you the mind begins nothing lofty. Come now,
break off all the sluggish delays, nod assent to bold beginnings.
Be here; let the mad waves beat the shores,
and if you can pause at all, rest beneath the shade
with me together in the woods: complete the task once taken up.
No glory will be sought in my affairs without you;
no songs shall I sing, [turning] toward the great city of Mars —
exempt from so great a war, [being] your chief care,
she herself stays unmoved, and fearless watches the battles.
Amid these upheavals, and contests so great,

div.note: For Fortune is depicted standing on a wave.
That is, in the verses of Virgil of Mantua.
Alludes to Fortune, who never rests.

lg.l: amid the arms of kings and the Latins bristling with war,
hail, true offspring of Jove, a godhead sacred to me,
you who keep watch over the Tuscan Tiber and the Roman palaces.
See, the nymphs bring you lilies in brimming baskets;
some beat out dances with their feet. You the greatest world —
author of the harvests and mistress of the seasons —
worships as a suppliant before the altars with a full incense-box.
Hail, great mother of the crops! You win over the scepters
and Jove himself; you grant us to recline at the banquets of the gods,
the shepherds of the flocks, and you lead [them] amid great rewards.
But the ancient race of Earth, the Titan brood,
with you as leader, cast down, are rolled in the lowest deep;
for the king of the sky-dwellers you aimed the darts and the hands,
and the brothers sworn together to tear open the sky
he thrust down, with thick wounds, to the Stygian waves,
and [into] the grove darkening with black dread,
the pale shades of Erebus. At you the doorkeeper of Orcus,
at you the Stygian lakes, have trembled; you slay the Cretan
prodigies, and the huge lion beneath the Nemean crag.
A companion to Alcides ever, so long as earth supplied
heavy labors, and let loose all the reins of her wrath —
the savage wife of Jove; and now, with so many years slipping by,
you turn the unwarlike Indian away from the Roman citadels,
and the Parthian who trusts in flight, and the double-tongued Tyrians;
[men] worn out by every mischance, destitute of all,
the Romans, lords of the world, you restore to their scepters.
From that time the honor has been kept: vows to you each year,
for whom our altars smoke twelve days,
we, being saved, perform; and we renew the deserved honors.
For what remains, I pray, may you confirm your divine presence closer at hand:

div.note: When Siena was besieged by Emperor Charles V, and defended by Henry II, King of France.
For they are shepherds born in a lowly station.
Saturn cast down the Titans, Jupiter the Giants,
...exalts the humble and casts down the proud (fragment).

lg.l: guard first this house, and the stern MOUNT;
let there be a Latium, let there be Alban kings through the ages,
let the descendants abide, chaste, in this observance.
You, Goddess, you at hand, come to the succor of our toil;
you instruct the bard, you, goddess, prompt: I shall tell of bristling wars
and great-hearted leaders — may it be granted to tell your deeds,
now, or one day, at whatever time strength shall offer itself.
Scarcely had I uttered this, when — poured suddenly around —
the cloud splits open, and there shone forth in clear light,
raising itself on its peak, the immovable rock of the Capitol.
The grove shuddered, and the rivers stayed their courses
at the Goddess's approach; the storm-clouds flee through the vast sky;
for very joy they hurl their voices to the stars,
the unshorn MOUNTS; the woods echo back everything.
At her coming, to sing a finely-drawn song
my mind stirs me, nor is it content with quiet repose:
the song of prophetic Manto, through the Roman towns,
I shall tell indeed; it delights to give rein to the mad labor.
A greater work, a greater train of things, is born for me.
I myself, my head adorned with the leaves of the trimmed olive,
returning, shall lead the Muses down from the Aonian height
along an unwonted path; I shall bring you back palms, Mantua,
unless my forebears, deluded, taught the augury in vain.

div.note: Alludes to the family, and to Pope Julius III himself, whose emblem is the Mount.
For the cento is made from Virgil.
Because apart from Eudocia, Proba, and Ausonius, no one else wrote centos.

lg.l: Hail, holy parent, whom the stars of heaven obey,
and the infernal lakes, and the walls of lofty Rome —
fortunate old man! If my songs have any power,
always shall your honor and your name and your praises remain.
Nor shall you go unsung in our songs,
son of the highest father; nor shall I pass you over in silence, O worthy of remembrance,
O glory of Italy, second hope of great Rome,
bearing again your grandsire's name. And with what song shall I tell of you,
be blessed in fresh valor, boy, as you seek new realms!
Born of gods and to beget gods: a wife is led home for you,
whose lineage from forebears [is] mighty, amid the rainy south winds.
Strew the ground with leaves, give lilies with full hands,
Laurentine nymphs; it is a joy to give oneself to the dances.
All things now smile; and you, O most holy wife,
hail, great mother, and [you,] twin sons at the breast;
Live happy, O three and four times blessed,
and the children of your children, and those who shall be born from them.

div.note: This cento should have been placed after the fourth one in this book.
New kingdoms, that is, Parma and Piacenza.
Margaret of Austria, daughter of Emperor Charles V, who gave birth to twins.

lg.l: If the opinion of the Samian seer [Pythagoras] is true, Laelius,
the soul that is now yours was formerly Maro's [Virgil's].
O priest outstanding in spirit, with your long robe,
flower and valour of the men of old, O divine Poet:
what gifts, what gifts shall I render you for such a song?
Ye gods, if there is any regard in heaven that cares for such things,
may they bring worthy rewards — to repay worthy thanks
is not in our power. It will be enough to tell your deeds,
now, one day, at whatever time strength shall offer itself.
What do I say? or where am I? what madness alters my mind?
Time carries all away; and with what song shall I tell of you,
now grown old [myself]? My tongue has no strength; nor do my body's wonted
powers suffice; labored panting shakes my limbs.
Yet I shall tell it, relying on the lyre and the tuneful strings
of prophetic Manto — if anyone, even so, if anyone,
seized by love, shall read these too, by the wave of the Tiber's stream,
every grove shall sing of you, you most observant of justice,
you, all the glory to your own, at the great city of Mars.
Yours is the care to guard the images of the gods and their temples,
and the sacred springs, and the heights over which high Apollo
presides, and with his song calls the gods to the contest.
Hail, true offspring of Jove, to whom songs are ever,
and the lyre, dear. While breath shall govern these limbs,
you shall ever be honoured by me, ever celebrated with gifts.
The End.

div.note: For he is a beneficiary (officeholder) of the Vatican basilica.

div.p: Antonio Possevino, a young man distinguished not only by sweetness and elegance of character but also by incredible learning, had published these Centos of Laelius Capilupi — marvelously fashioned out of Virgilian verses — which had been wrung from their author by almost daily importunities. Since Laelius, out of his singular goodwill toward men devoted to the good arts and to letters, had given me a number of copies of them to be bestowed, at my own discretion, upon men of letters, I judged Benedictus Aegius of Spoleto — whose learning and humanity are, I think, unknown to no one — not unworthy of so great a gift. He indeed, once he had read through the work, composed the distich set out above, fitted to this subject, and gave it to me to read; and when I had committed it to memory and, a little later, happened to meet Capilupo, I recited it to him. He at once, in return for the distich — such being his extraordinary memory, judgment, wisdom, and generosity, imitating the most fertile soil — composed a whole Cento in praise of B. Aegius in the space of scarcely an hour and a half. Wherefore, thinking I would be doing something worthwhile, I have willingly and gladly, on behalf of Antonio Possevino — by far the most devoted to me of all men, and to whom, because he was away,

it was not possible to finish the rest of the task — taken care, on this final page, to have this Cento likewise appended and printed in the same type, so that in this respect too provision might be made for the joint immortality of both friends. Farewell.
